tier_up_alt._note: Added key (C-cycle 47): extra Commander lines on a growth-tier rise, keyed by tier NAME exactly as in growth_tiers.tiers (3 per tier). Pick at random from this list plus the matching tier_up line. Same voice as 'says'. No new mechanics. Additive; dead until wired.
Crossing: 'Three huts and a river. Every city has an embarrassing beginning.'
'A fire, a ford, and a stubborn few. I have held worse with less.'
'Nothing here to guard yet. I guard it anyway. Practice.'
Hamlet: 'Chimneys. Chimneys mean people who intend to stay.'
'A hamlet. It has a name and a dog. It is nearly a town.'
'Walls will follow the roofs. They always do. I am prepared.'
The Guild Post: 'The guild has a door and a ledger. Now it can be disappointed on paper.'
'A post, a roster, a stamp. The paperwork of heroism begins.'
'Somebody will sign up who ought not to. That is how it starts.'
Village: 'A village. Now we have something to lose, and I like that. It sharpens a man.'
'Smoke from forty chimneys. Forty reasons to hold the road.'
'We have a green and a well. We shall be defending both.'
Market Day: 'A market. Now thieves have somewhere to be, and I know where to stand.'
'Stalls, scales, and the hum of coin. The gate will be busy.'
'Traders bring wealth and weather. I prepare for both.'
The Chapel: 'A chapel bell. Now the dead have an hour to rest in, and a reason to.'
'The priest has a roof. The roof has a vow. I shall be on the steps.'
'A chapel. I do not pray. I stand outside it, which counts for more.'
Craft Row: 'A row of smithies. Good. Steel is the only argument that wins.'
'Hammers from dawn. I sleep better on the sound of it.'
'The craftsmen have their own street. The guard shall have its own corner.'
The Garrison: 'A garrison. At last a proper barracks. I shall have my own bed, though I will not use it.'
'Bunks, a muster yard, a standing watch. Now we are an army with ambitions.'
'The garrison is raised. I shall say a few words, and you will wish I had said fewer.'
Market Town: 'A market town. The roads will fill. So will the ledgers, I fear.'
'Carts at every gate and coin in every pocket. Keep a hand on your purse and mine on my sword.'
'Everyone is passing through. Everyone is passing something along.'
The First Wall: 'A wall. A true one. I have waited years to lean on something that leans back.'
'Stone, finally. Now I shall have something to stand beside while I stand.'
'The First Wall. I walked its length twice before it was dry.'
Walled Town: 'Walled, gated, and watched. Bellmire at last has a shape.'
'A walled town now. Enemies shall have to be creative, and I shall have to be pleased.'
'The walls hold. The people feel it. That is half the defence, and the cheap half.'
City in all but Charter: 'A city in all but a paper. I shall wait for the paper. I have waited for worse.'
'Everything but the seal. The charter will arrive when somebody remembers to ask.'
'Bellmire. A city by every measure save the clerk's. I stand on the same gate I started on.'

e3po._note_c52: Widened C-cycle 52: 12 thinner pools gain 14 lines each (168 total): rank_up, trader_arrives, dispute, delve_dispatch, lord_cleared, drill, hurt, viewer_cosmetic, recruit, viewer_down, viewer_returns, lord_sighted. Same string shape as before; additive; dead until wired.
e3po._note_c59: Added lines (C-cycle 59): E3PO raid, disaster, festival, town_talk +12 each; viewer_roll crit/high/low/fumble +10 each; intro +6; says +8 (102 total). Appended to the existing lists, same string shape and voice. He still cannot die. Additive; dead until wired.

tier_up_alt2._note: Added key (C-120): a second set of Commander lines on a growth-tier rise, 4 per tier, keyed by tier NAME exactly as in growth_tiers.tiers (the same keys as tier_up_alt, which is untouched). Pick at random from tier_up, tier_up_alt and this list. Lower tiers are make-do; the later tiers are prosperous (glass, lamps, painted doors). No new mechanics. Additive; dead until wired.
Crossing: 'Two planks and a rope. I have defended less and been thanked for it.'
'A ford is a decision. Somebody made it here. I shall see it kept.'
'Nothing to take yet. That will not stop anyone trying.'
'A cookfire and a wet dog. It is a start, and I have started worse.'
Hamlet: 'A well, a pen, a lean-to. People who build a well mean to drink from it for years.'
'Smoke at dawn. I like a place that wakes up on purpose.'
'The children have found the ford. Someone ought to show them where it ends.'
'A hamlet. I shall learn the dogs by name first. They are the real watch.'
The Guild Post: 'A stamp on a ledger. It will outlast the first three heroes, I expect.'
'The door has a bell on it. Good. I want to hear who comes in.'
'A board for notices, and nobody yet to read them. That changes.'
'Sign here, bleed there. I shall tell the recruits about the second part.'
Village: 'A green, a well, a fence line. Something is worth walking round at night now.'
'Forty chimneys. I counted twice because I did not believe the first.'
'A village keeps a watch because it has bread worth stealing.'
'I know the names on every door. That is the thing a wall cannot do.'
Market Day: 'Scales on every stall. I shall learn which ones lie.'
'Coin changes hands and so does trouble. I stand where I can see both.'
'The caravan masters ask for me by name now. I did not ask for that.'
'Market day. Loud, crowded, and not one cart unguarded. Good.'
The Chapel: 'The bell has a rope and the rope has a boy. That is a bell with a future.'
'A roof for the dead and a pew for the tired. Both will be used.'
'The priest asked for a guard on the door. I said the door was already guarded.'
'Candles in the window. Somebody will see them from the road and know the way.'
Craft Row: 'The row smells of hot iron and fresh bread. I would defend either.'
'A glassblower, a cooper, a smith. Everything a siege needs, and nobody planning one.'
'Apprentices run between the shops. Quick feet. I will use them.'
'Honest work, three streets of it. I know what a raider sees.'
The Garrison: 'Whitewash on the barracks. Somebody was proud of this. Good.'
'A yard, a rack of spears, a roster. The Watch has a home now and a bad habit of staying in it.'
'Drill at dawn, stew at noon. A garrison runs on two things and I have both.'
'Real beds. I shall pretend not to notice who sleeps in them.'
Market Town: 'Cloth, salt, iron, wine. The road brings all of it and a few things we did not order.'
'There is a toll house now. Even the thieves complain about the prices.'
'The inn has a second floor. Somebody has money to spend on sleeping.'
'Painted shopfronts. A town that paints its doors expects to be around.'
The First Wall: 'Mortar still wet in the north run. I walked it anyway.'
'The gate has a name. A town names the things it means to keep.'
'Masons on the scaffold, bells on the hour. This is what a promise looks like built.'
'The wall is not high. It is not for height. It is for the people inside knowing where it stops.'
Walled Town: 'Banners on the towers, lamps on the wall. We have been seen from the road for a mile.'
'A garrison, a gate, a market, a bell. The pieces fit. I do not say that lightly.'
'The wall will be tested. That is what it is for. The gate is ready.'
'Good stone, good timber, good people. I would not trade the set.'
City in all but Charter: 'Glass in the windows and lamps in the streets. The charter can take its time.'
'Seven bells now, and every one rung on time. That is a city in my book.'
'I held the ford when there was no wall. I hold it now with all of this behind me. It is better.'
'Whatever the clerks call it, the gate is the same gate. The door is kept.'

town_life._note: Ambient Bellmire flavour as the town grows - crier calls, market and guild chatter, building news. For the desktop's town.gd if it wires a ticker; content worker never touches code. Additive; dead until wired.
crier: Grain measured, flasks counted, door kept - Bellmire stands another day!
Fresh off the river: trout, and a tale with every one.
The guild takes names at the post. Bring your own courage.
Lamps lit, walls walked, all's well - or well enough.
Another delver down the scar. Put a copper on them coming back up.
Walls walked, gates kept, and the bell has nothing to say!
Caravan on the road - bring coin or bring your back!
New names on the guild post. Read them while they are fresh.
The apothecary has flasks and the guild has holes to put them in!
Taxes measured, not guessed - the Hall says so.
Rain by evening. The crier is never wrong twice running.
Measure the grain, count the flasks, keep the door - and the crier keeps his voice!
Two up from the scar this morning, and both of them walking!
The bell has no clapper and even less to say. All's well!
Market day! Bring coin, bring elbows!
The Watch walked the wall twice and found nothing worth a second turn.
Flasks on the shelf, grain in the measure - Bellmire keeps its own accounts!
A lord came up out of the scar and went back down in pieces - hear it twice for a copper!
E3PO stood the night gate himself. Sleep easy, Bellmire.
Three down the scar before breakfast. The guild post is open and the ink is wet!
Stone on the road, masons on the wall - look lively or be built into it!
The Ford is running high. Cross at the ferry or cross at your own funeral!
Lost: one goat, answers to nothing. Found: one goat, answers to nobody!
The Hall sits at noon. Bring your grievance and bring it short!
Bandits on the west road, says the carter. Says it every week, mind.
Flasks counted twice today, on account of yesterday!
A caravan winters here, and the lanes are tight. Mind your elbows and your purse!
The night was quiet, the gate held, and the crier slept like an honest man!
New law posted at the Hall. Read it, or have it read to you at the gallows!
'Hear it, pay it, pass it on! Bellmire, your news!'
'Second bell! Any body with hands and a name, the drill yard calls!'
'Lost: one grey cat by the ford. Found: three. Come and argue!'
'Prices on the board, honest or you'll hear about it!'
'Third bell! Reeve wants a word at the Hall!'
'New rate on the toll - read it before you cross it!'
'Lost: a grey mare. Found: a grey mare. Not the same mare!'
'Bellmire sleeps well tonight, and E3PO sleeps better!'
Eight bells and all well! The ford is low, the gate is high, the guard is cross!
New names on the guild post! Come read them, and come add your own!
Lost: one goat, brown, answers to nothing. Found: the goat. Reward withdrawn.
The smith asks that no one lean on the new anvil. It is not set. It is not yet an anvil.
Market opens at the second bell! Count your coppers twice and your fingers three times!
The Commander says the wall is sound! The Commander says everything is sound! The Commander is correct!
Heard at the well: the scar was loud last night. Heard at the gate: it is always loud.
Bring your own bucket to the new well, and your own opinions to the old!
Ferry at the ford till dusk! The boatman is sober; the river is not!
A feast is promised and a fool is wanted for the middle of it! Apply at the chapel!
Every hero in Bellmire has a name here! Give yours at the post and be remembered!
Dark by the sixth bell and the lamps are lit! Walk in pairs, and let the lamps be yours!
Wall-work resumes at first light. Bring a trowel or bring a cart.
The mill turned a full day, and the flour was weighed honest.
A hero came home last night with all ten fingers. Bellmire counts that a good night.
Lamps lit at dusk along the whole market row, and nobody asked who paid.
Roof-tile and rope at the quay, the long barge in. Fair price for fair coin.
The bell rang for a wedding. Only the one this week, and it was a loud one.
Hearths banked, doors barred, children counted. Bellmire sleeps.
The well-wardens report the water sweet. Drink freely.
A fortnight without a funeral. Do not say it too loudly.
The guild post is open late. Bring a name, and bring a lantern.
The lamplighters ask for a spare ladder. Return the ladder.
Two barges at the quay and a third in sight. Mind your carts.
The wall-wardens will mend the east stair tomorrow. Use the west.
Rain by evening, say the ferrymen. Shutters, then.
A lost dog, brown, answers to nothing. Last seen at the bakery.
The tithe-clerk sits till dusk. He does not sit after dusk.
Fish at the ford and grain at the granary. Queue where the queue is.
The guild has paid out in full this week. Say thank you to the living.
market: Two coppers the carp, and the carp is grinning.
Dye by the ounce - name a colour, Bellmire keeps it now.
Scarglass! Cheap, and only slightly cursed!
Boots that have walked further than you have, half off.
Ale by the jug, and the jug is honest.
Nails, hooks, and a hammer that has seen things!
Salt off the coast road - you will taste the journey.
Wool off the hill, and it still smells of the hill.
Bread this morning; bread-shaped by this afternoon.
Lamp oil! Burns slow, and you will want the slow sort.
Rope by the fathom, and it has held a man before!
Scarstone, polished - it only looks at you a little!
Candles! Burn one for the delvers, buy two for yourself!
Hooks, lines, and a river that owes you nothing!
Cheese with a crust you could roof a barn with!
Fresh ink and honest parchment - write home while you still can!
A hat that has never once been rained on. Not once!
Secondhand steel - all of it came back up. Most of it alone.
Wax and wick! Burn one for the ones still down there!
Charcoal by the sack, and the sack is nearly full!
Thread, needles, and a patch for whatever the scar did to you!
Smoked river fish - it has been through worse than you have!
Horn cups, horn combs, horn everything - we had a good year for horns!
Pickles! Older than some of my customers!
Blankets off the hill flocks, thick enough to stand up on their own!
Boots resoled while you wait, and you will wait!
Honey when the hives are ours to take it from. Today they are!
Lanterns, hooks and a long pole - everything a man needs to not go in after it!
The baker's boy is undercutting his father two stalls down.
A fishwife has a crow in a cage. She is not selling it; she wants it on record.
The salt stall weighs twice and smiles once.
The potter will take a chipped cup in trade and knock a copper off.
The chandler has a second row of lanterns - the first is spoken for.
The miller's boy throws the weight twice, out of kindness.
A new stall - saltpans by the ford, and the salt knows it.
The dyer has a run of carrion that nobody will admit to buying.
Pickled eel, three coppers, and the eel has seen things.
Iron nails by the fistful, and every nail sworn to hold.
Wool, washed, and the sheep has been told to look surprised.
Candles! Tallow, wax, and one that burns blue and is not for sale.
Come buy a flask! It is full, it is red, and it is a great deal better than it looks.
Honest scales here. Ask any man who has been wrong about it.
Smoked fish! Smoked cheese! Smoked, I say, and the smoke was well spent!
Dyer's corner: any colour in the world, and several that are not.
Rope, hemp, forty feet, and a knot the guild swears by.
Fresh bread, warm, and I will not discuss the price until you have had a bite.
Charms against the scar, two coppers. They do nothing. They comfort a great deal.
Hats, hoods, and a fine plain cap. Be visible, be remembered, be dry.
Cheese from the high farms, still sharp. Ask for the rind.
Honest weights, honest scales. The scales are the town's, so check them yourself.
Linen by the yard, dyed in the new guild blue. Sells slow, wears long.
Hot pies at the corner, and the corner is crowded.
Rope, nails and good iron. The smith is in and the smith is short-tempered.
Fresh bread, and day-old bread at half. The day-old is the better bread.
Tallow, wicks, and a lamp-oil that does not stink.
Wool by the fleece, spun by the skein, and the spinner will tell you the price twice.
Apples from the east terrace. The last of the season, so take the lot.
Silver wire and plain rings, no scarglass. Honest work for the weddings.
Salt by the scoop, and pepper by the pinch. Pinch is a coin.
Candle-ends cheap, for reading late.
Barley loaves, rye loaves, and a seed loaf the baker is proud of.
Cheese from the high pasture. Sharp, and sold by the wedge.
Leather straps, new and mended, and the cobbler's boy asleep behind them.
Smoked eel on a string, a copper the length of your hand.
Honey in clay pots. Bring the pot back, get a copper.
Ironmonger's seconds: good nails, bent heads, half price.
growth: The masons raised a new course on the wall today.
A second well dug, and the queue at the first one shorter.
They are building where the fields used to stop.
The guild post has two doors now. Both kept.
The smith has an apprentice, and the apprentice has eyebrows. For now.
A proper gate, hung and swinging true.
The road out is cobbled as far as the ford.
They are putting glass in the chapel windows.
A second row of stalls, and a queue for them.
The barracks took on ten more. E3PO looked almost pleased.
The ditch is dug, the stakes are in, and the masons are measuring stone.
A new row of chimneys on the east side, all of them smoking.
They have hung a lamp at the ford. It burns all night now.
The guild post took on a clerk, and the clerk took on a queue.
A tannery, downwind - and the town voted on which wind.
The market square has flagstones where the mud was.
A second smith, and the two of them already disagree.
They are cutting a road where the fields used to stop.
They have roofed the old well, and the water tastes of less sky.
A stone granary going up by the Hall, and the masons will not say how much.
Drains under the high street. The town smells of digging instead of worse.
The chapel has a clapper on order, and opinions arriving free.
A second gate cut in the north wall, because the first one had a queue.
The guild post painted its door. The door is still kept.
A bath house, of all things, and a line outside it already.
They are laying a wharf at the Ford, long enough for two boats to argue over.
The yard has a practice dummy that E3PO himself broke in half. They built a stronger one.
Lamps the whole length of the high street now. The dark stops at the wall.
Another roof goes up; another kettle gets hung.
The ward lists a new name. Nobody argues it.
A second well is being dug, and a first argument is being had over it.
Market Day has outgrown its square. The square is being argued with.
The crier is paid a second copper for the second bell.
A third guild post opens, and already the clerk is tired.
The wall ward lists two new names, and argues about a third.
Lanterns the length of the ford now. The low field can see its own grain.
A roof went up on Cobbler's Lane in a day, and the day was well spent.
The ferry has a second boat, and the first boat is looking at it nervously.
They are paving the square. The old mud will be missed by nobody but the pigs.
New smoke over the east side - three chimneys where there was one.
The guild post has a new shutter. It closes. It is considered a luxury.
Another baker has opened, and the first baker is being very polite about it.
The ditch by the wall has been dug deeper, to the guard's great satisfaction.
A second lantern at the gate, and the dark is a little thinner for it.
The chapel bell was rehung, and for the first time it rings on the hour.
Carts roll in from the west road with more timber, more nails, and more rumour.
Someone planted flowers at the guild post. They survived. This is a good sign.
A new family came down the road and took the empty house. It is no longer empty.
New thatch on the east row, and the old thatch carted off for the cattle.
The mason's boy has his own chisel now, and his own corner.
A second market day has been added, and the stalls have filled it already.
They paved the lane to the guild post. The mud has to go somewhere else.
Another smithy has opened by the ford. The first smithy is not pleased.
A bell has been hung where the old wall stood. The wall moved out a bowshot.
Stone houses along the river now, where there were reed huts last year.
The ferry has a roof, and the ferryman a bench.
The granary has a lock, and the lock has a second key.
A school on the green. It has two benches and an excellent door.
The mill has a second wheel, and the miller a second apprentice.
Cobbles reached the tanners' lane this month. The tanners have opinions.
A fountain on the green. It runs. People stand and watch it run.
The wall-wardens have a proper hut now, with a stove.
The ford has a bridge, and the ferryman a grudge.
Lamp-posts on the high street, one to a house. The lamplighter is delighted.
The inn has added a second floor and a second chimney. Both draw.
A new bell for the quay, so the barges are counted in.

propositions._note: Viewer-voting town laws (T4). 17 across law/taxes/militia/building/faith/outsiders. Each names a CONSEQUENCE, good and bad - a law that only helps is boring. Readable at a glance. Dead until wired.

entries.title: The Gallows Law
entries.flavour: Thieves hang, not fine. The guild says it will clear the market of cutpurses.
entries.good: Crime falls; the market feels safe to spend in.
entries.bad: The desperate turn to worse than theft, and some good hands leave town.

entries.title: Trial by the Roll
entries.flavour: Let the accused delve the scar. Come back up, and you walk free.
entries.good: Wildly popular on stream, and the dungeon runs hot.
entries.bad: The innocent die below, and the guild loses good names.

entries.title: Debtors' Pardon
entries.flavour: Wipe the slate. Come spring, no one in Bellmire owes a copper.
entries.good: The poor breathe again; loyalty climbs.
entries.bad: The lenders shut their purses, and coin stops moving.

entries.title: Raise the Grain Tithe
entries.flavour: A heavier cut of every harvest goes to the town coffers.
entries.good: The treasury swells; walls and wages get paid.
entries.bad: Full barns, thin bellies - the folk grumble, and some go hungry.

entries.title: The Free Market Charter
entries.flavour: Drop the market tolls. Any trader sells in Bellmire toll-free.
entries.good: Caravans flock in; the stalls overflow.
entries.bad: The coffers thin, and the guild's grip slips.

entries.title: Toll at the Ford
entries.flavour: A copper to cross, paid to the Ferryman, paid to the town.
entries.good: Steady coin off every crossing.
entries.bad: Traders grumble, some ford downstream, and the Ferryman is not thanked.

entries.title: Raise the Militia Levy
entries.flavour: Every household sends a hand to the wall.
entries.good: The guard doubles; raiders think twice.
entries.bad: Fewer hands in the fields - the town is safer but poorer.

entries.title: Arm the Delvers
entries.flavour: Guild steel for anyone who will hold the gate.
entries.good: A hard town to raid.
entries.bad: Armed and idle men make their own trouble.

entries.title: Night Curfew
entries.flavour: Lamps out, doors barred, the Watch walks till dawn.
entries.good: No raid slips in by night.
entries.bad: The taverns empty; the folk feel watched, not kept.

entries.title: Wall the Town
entries.flavour: Stone where the fields stop. The masons are ready and waiting.
entries.good: Bellmire holds against any raid.
entries.bad: It costs a fortune, and the harvest waits while the masons build.

entries.title: Dig the Second Well
entries.flavour: One well, long queues, and the dry months coming.
entries.good: Water for all, even in a drought.
entries.bad: The diggers want paying, and they keep hitting scarstone.

entries.title: Pave the Market Square
entries.flavour: Mud to flagstone, fit for a city.
entries.good: Traders linger; the town looks the part.
entries.bad: A whole season's coin, sunk into the ground.

entries.title: Ring the Festival
entries.flavour: A feast day on the guild's coin, and the clapperless bell rung anyway.
entries.good: Spirits soar; both loyalty and trade rise.
entries.bad: A day's work lost, and a day's coin with it.

entries.title: Tithe to the Chapel
entries.flavour: Fund the temple and light every candle.
entries.good: The faithful are glad; the sick are tended.
entries.bad: Coin the walls could have used.

entries.title: Open the Gates to Refugees
entries.flavour: Folk fleeing the scar-lands crowd the Ford by the hundred.
entries.good: New hands for the fields and the wall.
entries.bad: More mouths to feed - and sickness travels with them.

entries.title: Hire the Sellswords
entries.flavour: Coin for blades that answer to gold, not the guild.
entries.good: Hard muscle for the hard floors.
entries.bad: They stay bought only as long as you keep paying.

entries.title: Shut the Border
entries.flavour: No stranger past the Ford without the guild's word.
entries.good: No raider walks in wearing a traveller's coat.
entries.bad: Trade withers, and the town turns inward and small.

entries.title: The Honest Measure
entries.flavour: Every weight in the market checked at the Hall, and stamped, or smashed.
entries.good: Buyers trust the stalls; market takings and the town cut both rise.
entries.bad: The sharper traders take their carts to an easier road, and stalls stand empty a while.

entries.title: Blood Price
entries.flavour: A killing is settled in coin paid to the family, not in rope.
entries.good: Feuds end at the Hall instead of in the street; fewer good hands are lost.
entries.bad: A rich man can afford a murder, and everyone in town can do the sum.

entries.title: Chain Them to the Wall
entries.flavour: Taken bandits work the wall instead of hanging from it.
entries.good: Building goes faster and costs the town nothing in wages.
entries.bad: Armed men guarding chained men; now and then a chain comes off at night.

entries.title: The Delver's Tithe
entries.flavour: One part in ten of everything carried up the scar, paid at the post.
entries.good: The treasury fills whenever the dungeon runs hot.
entries.bad: Delvers hide the best of it, and some sell to the Ford instead of the guild.

entries.title: Hearth Tax
entries.flavour: Every chimney in Bellmire pays, counted from the wall on a cold morning.
entries.good: Steady coin that does not care whether the dungeon pays out this week.
entries.bad: The poorest let their fires go out to go uncounted, and the winter takes some of them.

entries.title: The Scarglass Levy
entries.flavour: Tax what comes out of the scar as glass, not as gold.
entries.good: The oddities pay their way, and the apothecary gets first refusal on stock.
entries.bad: Scarglass goes under the counter; smuggling takes root at the Ford.

entries.title: Drill Every Seventh Day
entries.flavour: Every able hand in the yard one day in seven. E3PO calls the time.
entries.good: The militia holds a line instead of breaking; raid losses drop sharply.
entries.bad: A day in seven out of the fields and workshops - everything else comes slower.

entries.title: The Night Horn
entries.flavour: A horn hung in every quarter, and a standing order to blow it first and ask after.
entries.good: The town turns out fast; raids are met at the gate rather than in the square.
entries.bad: False alarms most weeks, and a town that sleeps badly works badly.

entries.title: Muster the Farmhands
entries.flavour: The outlying holdings send one hand each to the garrison for the season.
entries.good: The garrison stands at full strength through the dangerous months.
entries.bad: Harvest comes in short-handed, and the holdings remember who asked.

entries.title: Roof the Market
entries.flavour: Timber and tile over the square, so market day happens whatever the sky does.
entries.good: Market day never cancels; trade income steadies across the whole year.
entries.bad: Costly, and a roofed square burns as one thing instead of twenty.

entries.title: Dig the Drains
entries.flavour: Stone drains under the streets, downhill, away from the well.
entries.good: Sickness drops and the town stops stinking in summer; growth comes easier.
entries.bad: Months of open trench through the middle of everything, and the cost of every yard of it.

entries.title: Raise a Granary
entries.flavour: A stone granary by the Hall, kept full against a bad year.
entries.good: A failed harvest or a burned field no longer means a hungry winter.
entries.bad: Grain sits idle that could have been sold, and a full granary is a target worth raiding.

entries.title: Hang a Clapper in the Bell
entries.flavour: The bell has rung without one since the tower went up. The chapel wants it finished.
entries.good: A bell that carries - the town hears a raid called from any field it works.
entries.bad: Some swear the bell was better unfinished, and the old families take it badly.

entries.title: Bring the Delvers Home
entries.flavour: The town pays to carry its dead up out of the scar and bury them in daylight.
entries.good: Delvers go down easier knowing it; the guild post never wants for names.
entries.bad: A steady drain of coin, and parties that turn back carrying a body instead of loot.

entries.title: Winter the Caravans
entries.flavour: Let the road traders keep their carts inside the wall until the thaw.
entries.good: Goods and coin stay in Bellmire all winter, and the spring road opens from here.
entries.bad: Crowded lanes, strained stores, and outsiders who learn the inside of the wall by heart.

disasters._note: Natural disasters (D34). For each: begin (Chronicle line), during (lines while it lasts), pass (line when it ends), cost (plain statement of what it should cost the town, for the desktop to implement). Dead until wired.
disasters._note_variants: Added C-cycle 11: begin_alt and pass_alt (arrays) sit beside begin and pass on EVERY disaster, and during is widened to 8 lines each. begin/pass are unchanged and still the single canonical line - a picker may roll begin_alt/pass_alt instead so a second volcano does not read word for word like the first. Additive; dead until wired.

volcano.begin: The mountain above the scar wakes - ash on the wind, and the sky goes copper.
during: Ash falls on Bellmire; the sun is a dull coin behind the smoke.
The river runs grey, and the fish float up dead.
Cinders tick off the roof-tiles all night; nobody opens a shutter.
The crier reads the day's news through a cloth over his mouth.
The ash drifts into the grain store through a gap nobody knew was there.
Sheep come down off the high pasture coughing, and do not go back up.
The chapel bell rings muffled, packed with grey.
Children write their names in the ash on the shutters. By morning it has written over them.
A cart leaves two clean ruts in the grey, and nothing else does.
The guild post sells cloth masks and is out of them by noon.
Lamps are lit at midday; the copper sky gives nothing to work by.
Ash sits a finger deep on the chapel steps and is swept twice a day.
Grey settles on the market bread, and the bread sells anyway.
The high pasture is gone under ash; the shepherds bring everything down.
Ash falls like grey snow and the cookfires are put out to save the air.
The mountain speaks again and every bell in Bellmire answers it badly.
Carts queue at the Ford with everything a household can lift.
The water butts are skimmed twice a day and still run grey.
A roof goes in under the weight of its own ash, and nobody was under it.
The crier's voice carries badly; the ash eats it before the far side of the square.
The guild post weighs ash out of the grain and charges for honest weight.
Every doorstep is swept, and every doorstep is grey again by dusk.
The forge works blind, the smoke of its own making lost in the bigger smoke.
Bellmire counts the flasks early this week, because the lamps burn all day.
A crust of ash forms on every water barrel by noon.
The forges damp down - no sense feeding a fire the mountain is already feeding.
Children are kept indoors; a mask of linen goes with any errand.
Horses baulk at the grit and will not be led out of the stable.
The guild post marks a line through market day.
The clapperless bell wears a cowl of grey by evening.
Ash lies in the well-rope and the bucket comes up gritty.
The mill-wheel turns slower, clogged with grey.
Nobody can tell noon from dusk; the lamplighter gives up.
A hen lays an egg dusted pale as flour.
The smith spits grey and keeps hammering, for spite.
Fine ash in the ale. The tavern charges the same.
Ash lies on the washing line, and on the washing.
The Watch wear wet rags over the face and call the hours hoarse.
Ewes stand in the pens with grey wool and will not eat.
The bellringer climbs the tower by feel; the lamps do not carry in this.
Ash on the washing before it is dry. The washing is brought in and shaken.
The mountain mutters. The dogs have gone under the cart-sheds and will not come out.
Grey on every sill, grey on every hat. The sweeps have given up.
Ash in the well-bucket, ash in the soup. The market opens anyway.
Roofs are raked clean of ash before the next rain makes it cement.
volcano.pass: The mountain settles. Ash greys every roof, but the air clears.
volcano.cost: A buried harvest and sickened livestock; the worst-hit district must be rebuilt.
begin_alt: Grit on the tongue before dawn - the mountain is awake, and the sky turns copper.
The mountain clears its throat. Ash comes down on Bellmire like slow snow.
Ash on the wind out of the high country. Shutter the stores.
The mountain wakes above the scar, and the first ash reaches the square by noon.
Copper sky, grit in the water butt. The mountain has started.
Smoke stands over the high country in a column, and the column is leaning this way.
The mountain opens, and the sky over Bellmire turns the colour of a bruise.
Ash on the wind before dawn - the mountain has decided something.
The high country lights from underneath, and the wind brings the first grey.
Thunder with no cloud. The mountain is clearing its throat again.
The water butts skin over grey before breakfast. It has started.
A red seam opens on the mountain's shoulder and the sky closes over it.
The mountain lifts a column of smoke, and the column points at Bellmire.
First ash by first light. The crier is told to speak through cloth.
The high pasture goes under grey before the shepherds are awake.
The mountain burns somewhere inside itself, and Bellmire gets the smoke.
The mountain sends its warning on the wind - grit between the teeth before the sun is up.
Copper sky. Copper taste. The scar is not the only thing in Bellmire with a temper.
Ash in the mornings' bread before anyone has baked. The mountain is lit.
The sky above the mountain goes the colour of a struck forge, and holds there.
The watchman on the north wall whistles once and points. That is enough.
A tremor runs the Ford, and the mountain answers with smoke.
Every dog in Bellmire howls at the same mountain, the same minute.
A tremor in the cups, a rumble in the floor, and the peak lights red.
The scar's old neighbour wakes, and has opinions about the town.
A thump from the mountain, a second, and then the sky is the wrong colour.
Ash drifts down at noon. By dusk it is deep enough to track a boot in.
The mountain above the scar clears its throat, and it is not a small throat.
Ash on the washing line, and nobody takes it in.
The mountain talks all night, low, and the dogs will not settle.
pass_alt: The mountain goes quiet. Bellmire shovels grey off its roofs and breathes clean.
The ashfall stops. Every rooftop wears a winter nobody ordered.
The sky loses its copper. The sweeping will take a month.
The column over the mountain thins and comes apart. It is finished.
The last grey flake lands. Bellmire starts at the roofs and works down.
The air comes clean again, one street at a time.
The mountain quiets. Ash lies a thumb deep on every roof that is left.
It is over. The town digs itself out grey to the knee.
The seam on the mountain closes. The shovels come out and stay out.
No new grey since dawn. Bellmire counts its roofs and starts lifting.
The smoke stands straight again, then not at all. It is done.
The sky lets the sun through, thin and ordinary, and the town cheers it.
The ash stops. Every gutter in town is packed and every gutter gets dug.
The mountain banks its fire. Grey to the knee, and all of it to move.
Clean air off the river at last. The grey goes back up the hill in carts.
It is over. The grain store is opened and the counting starts.
The mountain holds its breath. Bellmire does not, and scrubs.
The ashfall thins to nothing. The brooms come out before the sun.
A clean wind off the Ford, at last, and the roofs give up their grey.
The sky goes blue again - grudgingly, like a debt paid.
The forges wake. The smiths test the air and nod.
Bellmire sweeps its own eaves and calls it a holiday.
The last cinder ticks out. Bellmire shakes its hats and starts sweeping.
The sky pales from copper to honest grey. Folk breathe, and cough, and breathe.
The mountain sleeps again. The town does not trust it, and shouldn't.
The ash stops falling. Every roof is grey and every well needs skimming.
The mountain goes quiet. The sun comes back, small and white.
The last cinder ticks down. The town gets out the brooms.
Ash lies in the gutters. The Watch sweeps it from the bridge and says nothing.
The mountain quiets. Bellmire shakes out its blankets.

fire.begin: Fire in Craft Row - a forge banked wrong, and the wind unkind.
during: The bucket line runs from the river; the Watch beats at the flames.
Smoke rolls over the square as the smiths' roofs go up.
Craft Row is a tunnel of heat; the Watch wets the next roof down and waits.
Somebody's apprentice runs back in for the tools and is dragged out again.
The wind turns, and the bucket line turns with it, cursing.
A roof-beam goes down and the whole square flinches.
They pull a smith off his own forge; he fights them the whole way out.
Sparks ride the night air toward the thatch, and every eye follows them up.
They pull down the shed between the forge and the next roof to starve it.
Buckets come up the line faster than hands can empty them.
A smith's tools glow in the ruin, too hot to carry for an hour.
Somebody counts heads in the square, twice, and then a third time.
The wind drops, and the bucket line gains a yard on it.
Soot comes off the Row and settles on the washing three streets away.
The chapel bell rings itself hoarse and nobody is spare to stop it.
They run a wet line of cloth along the next row and dare the fire to cross it.
A child is handed up the bucket line and over the heads to the far side.
The bucket line runs from the river to Craft Row and does not break.
A roof is pulled down on purpose, to stop the fire using it as a road.
Soot in the bread, soot in the ale, and the market sells both.
The smiths stand in the square with their tools and nowhere to put them.
The chapel bell rings for the line to change hands.
The guild post hands out wet sacking and writes down every one.
Somebody carries the ledgers out before the furniture, and is thanked for it.
Sparks ride the wind as far as the chapel roof; a boy on the bellrope watches for them.
Doors are left wide so the bucket line runs through, not around.
Someone's cat is handed out a window, cursing.
A second row catches - the wind has made up its mind.
The apothecary pours his own water and shuts the door against the smoke.
A ledger is thrown from a shutter and lands open in the mud.
The bucket line runs from the well to the Row, and nobody rests.
Sparks hop the lane onto a dry thatch. A shout, a splash, a close one.
The smiths drag anvils out of the heat like wounded friends.
Smoke rolls over the market; the crier calls the wards by name.
A roof beam goes with a sound like a great door closing.
The bell clangs fire-time and every hand in town answers.
The wet-sack line holds the lane; the smiths wet their own doors and stand on them.
A thatch goes up in one breath and the lane leans back from it.
The bucket line has been passing for an hour. Nobody has said a word.
Coal-dust is carried out of the cellars before it can be a second fire.
The smiths drag their anvils into the lane so the roof will not have them.
A shutter burns off its hinge and drops. Nobody looks up from the line.
The well at the corner is dry by noon. The river line begins.
The line passes buckets hand to hand until the hands are raw.
Somebody keeps the tally of lost tools aloud, to keep from counting anything worse.
fire.pass: The fire is out. A row of workshops is char and cinder.
fire.cost: Buildings in one district burned down and rebuilt from nothing; the smiths sit idle until then.
begin_alt: Craft Row is alight - a banked forge, a bad wind, and no rain since market day.
Fire. The word crosses the square faster than the smoke does.
Flame in the workshops, and the Watch are up before the bell is.
A roof in Craft Row takes light, and the wind takes an interest.
The forge was banked wrong, and Craft Row is paying for it.
Fire in the workshops. The square fills before the bell is finished.
A spark finds the thatch, and thatch has no patience at all.
Fire in the Row - and the wind had been waiting all week for it.
Fire in Craft Row, and the wind has picked a direction.
Smoke off the workshops, and the bucket line forms before the bell.
A forge went up with the wind behind it. Craft Row is burning.
Flame in the roof-thatch, and the roofs here touch.
Fire takes a workshop, then its neighbour, then it stops asking.
Sparks in the thatch and no rain since the thaw. Craft Row is alight.
The bucket line is out before the smoke clears the ridge-tiles.
A banked forge woke in the night. Craft Row is the colour of a forge.
Smoke on the Craft Row wind - a forge banked wrong and a day that will not forgive it.
A shout from the row, and then a louder one. Fire finds words faster than most.
The chapel bell goes before the alarm bell does. Somebody there has a nose for it.
Craft Row lights up at the end nearest the river - which is lucky, and not enough.
The wind turns, and Bellmire learns the word for it again.
Fire. The bucket line is already forming by the time the call is through.
A glow in the wrong window - the Row's banked forge is no longer banked.
The wind turns, and the spark finds the oak shavings. Bellmire runs.
Smoke at the Row, and the first bucket already empty.
A bellows spark and a dry lane. Craft Row has about a minute's warning.
Smoke from the nail-maker's, and then from the wheelwright's next door.
Fire in Craft Row at the dinner hour, when every hearth is lit and every hand is at table.
Smoke over Craft Row before the noon bell, and the bell is rung early.
A spark, a dry roof, and the Row is on its feet shouting.
pass_alt: The last roof falls in and stays down. The fire is finished.
The flames are beaten out at the row's end. What is left is char and cinder.
It is over. Craft Row smokes, and the smiths stand looking at it.
They beat the last of it out at the Row's end as the sun comes up.
The fire is done. The Row stands in black timber and nobody speaks.
Out at last - and the count of people comes back whole. The buildings did not.
Black beams, white ash, and the bucket line still passing nothing.
The fire gives up before the town does. It usually does.
The last of it is beaten out. Craft Row is black, and standing.
The fire is put down at the lane's end. It took the row and stopped there.
Wet black timber and no flame. The smiths start again from nothing.
It is out. Bellmire counts the roofs it has left and gets to work.
The bucket line stands down. The row is ash, and nobody is missing.
The wind turned, and the fire had nowhere to go. It is finished.
Rain, late and welcome. The fire drowns in it.
Out by morning. The guild post opens its ledger on what is owed.
The last wall falls and takes the fire with it. Bellmire breathes out.
The row is black and wet. The Watch sits down where it stood.
Smoke drifts off the Ford. The tally begins.
The flames are out. The silence after is loud enough for everyone.
A roof falls in at dawn and nobody flinches - the fire was finished hours ago.
The buckets go back to the wells, one by one, dented and sooted.
The last roof falls in, and the flames have nothing left to eat.
Rain would have helped. Grit and sweat did the work instead.
The Row smoulders to black. The smiths count their tongs.
The fire is out. The Row is black to the lane's edge and no further.
It burns down to embers by noon. The smiths walk in and kick the ash for iron.
The last wet sack goes down on the last hot beam. Done.
The last ember is drowned. The smiths walk the char and count what is left.
The smoke thins. The bucket line sits down where it stood.

drought.begin: No rain since the thaw. The river drops, and the wells go shy.
during: The crops stand yellow and brittle in the field.
The queue at the well starts before dawn.
The mill-wheel stands still in a riverbed of stones.
Dust comes off the fields in sheets and settles on the market bread.
The well rope goes down further each morning and comes up lighter.
Dust walks the cart-track where the mud used to be.
The miller stops the wheel. There is no water to turn it.
Cattle are driven to the Ford and find it ankle-deep.
The Ford can be crossed dry-shod, and nobody is pleased about it.
Water is carted from upriver and sold by the bucket.
The fields crack into plates you could lift out whole.
The chapel prays for rain at every bell, and the bell is busy.
Thunder at dusk and no rain under it. That is the cruellest part.
The garden plots are given up so the grain can drink.
The river shows its bones at the Ford and the ferryman walks across.
Water is rationed by the bucket and counted by the chapel.

Meltwater comes down the valley in a single night. The river forgets where its banks are.
The river runs brown and fast, carrying fence posts. Someone says 'flood' and is not argued with.
The thaw lets go all at once, and the Ford goes under before the bells can be rung.
Water in the low lanes by morning. The river has decided to be a lake.
The snowmelt arrives like an army. The river climbs the bank and starts on the stairs.
A grey surge comes down off the hills. The low district hears it before it sees it.
The river brims, then spills, then simply comes to call.
Spring meltwater arrives like a debt collector, all at once.
The Ford sinks under the river, and the ferryman shrugs.
The river is a hand up at dawn, a foot at noon, and still climbing.
The thaw and a week of rain have met, and Bellmire is where they meet.
Water comes up through the cellar floors before it comes over the bank.
The Ford is under. The river is in the lower lane and the lane is not complaining.
Sandbags go down in a line along the bank and the water looks them over.
pass_alt: The water drops back. Mud in every doorway, and the town held.
The river goes home. It left most of its bed in Bellmire's front rooms.
The flood falls away. The Ford shows its posts again, and the trade with them.
The river falls back inside its banks and leaves the mud as rent.
The water goes. Every doorway in the low district needs a shovel.
The Ford shows its stones again, and the first cart over is cheered.
The water goes down and leaves the river's silt in every ground-floor room.
It drains. The smell will be with the lower streets for a month.
The river goes back inside its banks. Mud everywhere else.
The water falls. The Ford shows its posts and the carts queue up.
It drains away. Every ground floor in the low district is shovelled out.
The river retreats and leaves the town a thumb of silt as a souvenir.
Down at last. The grain store counts what got wet and what did not.
The flood lets go. The Ford opens and the trade comes back thirsty.
The water is off the lanes. The doors are left open to dry.
Over. The mud is scraped into the river that brought it.
The river slinks back to its bed, leaving silt on every sill and a fish in the chapel.
The water falls a hand a day, then a foot. By week's end the Ford is a Ford again.
The river retreats. Bellmire bails, scrapes, and counts what the mud kept.
The flood goes out the way it came, in the night, with whatever was not nailed down.
The low district surfaces. Every cellar is a pond, but the town stood.
Mud to the knee and sun on the water. The flood is done.
The water falls back, and leaves a silt-carpet on everything.
Mud, mud, mud, and the smell of wet river; the town starts shovelling.
The Ford resurfaces, a little sheepish, and the ferryman goes back to being a ferryman.
The river drops. The marks on the gatepost are cut in with a knife.
Mud is shovelled out into the lane, and the lane is shovelled into the river.
The Ford shows its stones. Carts line up, and the first through is cheered.
The river goes home. It leaves a brown line on every wall to show where it was.
Mud, to the knee, in every riverside shop. They start with shovels.

blight.begin: A black rot is in the grain - it came up in one field and did not stop there.
during: Whole rows are cut and burned before the rot can walk to the next field.
The miller turns away sack after sack, and says nothing, which is worse.
The rot shows black at the stalk and climbs from there.
Field hands burn their gloves at the end of the day, just in case.
Bread goes up a copper, then another, and the baker stops apologising.
The guild post buys grain from downriver at a price it will not read aloud.
A farmer stands at his field edge all afternoon doing nothing at all.
They plough the worst acre under and sow nothing in it.
The smoke of burning rows hangs over the fields all week.
Seed grain is set aside and guarded, because next year is in the sack.
A field is written off at noon and burned by dusk.
The baker mixes in what he can and calls it bread, generously.
Hands are scrubbed at the field gate before anyone walks home.
Downriver grain comes up the road under guard and is counted twice.
The fields go black in patches that spread while you watch them.
They burn one field to save the next and argue about it for years after.
The apothecary tests the grain and will not say what she found.
Infected fields are burned, deliberately, with the whole town watching.
Grain prices climb at the market and are read out anyway.
The seed corn is locked and a guard is put on the lock.
Traders come upriver with grain and name a price nobody likes.
The reeve walks the rows daily, marking what is still clean.
Bread is smaller this week and will be smaller next week.
The stores are measured twice, by two different people, in public.
Smoke from the burn-lines hangs over the farms.
The reapers cut ahead of the rot, and lose the race row by row.
Seed-grain is hidden in cellars; the Watch is told to look the other way.
Every field gets a ditch around it and a prayer inside it.
Bread is cut thinner. The bakers say nothing, loudly.
The apothecary swears the rot is not catching. The farmers burn their boots.
The rot creeps through the grain row by row, black and silent.
Farmers burn the worst plots and stand watching the smoke.
The mill sits idle; nothing sound is left to grind.
The market loaf has gone small, and the price has not.
A sour smell lies on the fields at dusk and refuses to leave.
Folk check each ear of corn like a bad coin.
Black stalks are carried to the burning pit in sacks, and the sacks are burned too.
The miller will not take a grain that has been near the north field.
Crows will not land on the blighted rows, and that says enough.
The farmers walk their rows each dawn, looking for the first black spot.
The rot is black at the root and sweet at the top. Do not eat it.
The field is walked end to end and all of it is the same.
The reeve burns the first row himself, and nobody else is asked.
Black smoke from the field-edge fires lies along the valley all day.
The millers refuse any grain they have not rubbed between their own fingers.
blight.pass: The blight burns out at the field edge. What is left of the harvest comes in early.
blight.cost: Most of the standing harvest is lost; food prices climb and the stores do not refill this season.
begin_alt: Black rot in the grain. It started in one field and did not stay there.
The harvest has something in it, and the something is spreading.
A blight walks the fields row by row, taking its time.
The grain blackens at the stalk in one field, and then in the next.
A rot comes up in the barley and starts to travel.
The harvest has gone wrong in a way the old farmers recognise.
Something is in the crop, and it moved from one furrow to the next overnight.
The barley goes grey at the edges, field by field.
Black rot in the grain, and it did not stay in the one field.
The standing crop goes dark at the root and spreads along the rows.
A rot in the ears. The reeve walks the fields and comes back quiet.
The grain is black where it should be gold, field after field.
Something is in the crop, and it is in all of the crop by week's end.
The blight shows up at the field edge and works inward.
The harvest turns dark on the stalk and nobody can stop it.
Rot in the grain, and the barns are told to expect less.
The leaves curl black overnight. The first field is lost and the second is going.
A rot with no name takes the grain at the root. The farmers burn their own fields and weep at the smoke.
Black spots on the ears, then black ears, then black fields. Measure the grain, and be quick.
The harvest was good for one morning. By dusk it was the colour of soot.
The reapers bring in sheaves that crumble to dust in the hand.
Something is wrong with the wheat, and it is catching.
A single black ear in a gold field, then ten, then the row.
The blight whispers in with the morning dew and takes the east field first.
The reeve cuts one stalk open, and swears.
One black ear in the north field. By night, forty.
The rot shows at the stalk-foot, soft and sour. The farmer burns his boots.
A grey mould on the barley, and then the smell.
The grain-heads are black to the root, and the field smells sweet and wrong.
The reeve walks a row of rot and tears off a stalk, and it crumbles.
pass_alt: The blight stops at the field edge. What is left comes in early and thin.
The rot burns out. Bellmire salvages whatever the fire did not reach.
It ends. The barns take a half-harvest and are told to make it do.
The last blackened row burns, and the rot has nowhere left to go.
The blight stops. What came in is thin, early and ours.
It burns out at the hedge. The barns take half of what was promised.
It stops at the burned line. What is left is harvested nervously.
The blight dies back. So has a third of the harvest.
The rot burns out with the stubble. Next year's seed is clean.
The blight is done. The fields are bare and the ground is sound.
It is over. What was saved is counted and the price settles.
The last black field is burned. The smoke smells like a bad year ending.
The rot stops at the fallow. The seed corn is clean and guarded.
The blight dies with the frost. The barns are short but honest.
Finished. The reeve walks clean rows and says so in the square.
The fields are cleared and limed. The next sowing is already argued over.
The rot stops at the ditch and goes no further. The surviving rows are cut green.
The last black field is burned. The smoke tastes of a bad year.
The blight burns itself out. What stands is cut early, bound thin and counted twice.
The wind turns and the rot does not follow. Bellmire salvages what it can.
The burning ends. The fields are ash, with a few green stripes.
The blight is done. The granary keeps a tally nobody enjoys reading.
The rot stops at the burned strip, as if it had read the warning.
What the blight left is brought in fast, and counted with grim thanks.
The black fades from the leaf; the surviving rows stand up, thin but clean.
The last blackened row is burned. The rest is thin, but sound.
The rot stops at the hedge. What is behind it is brought in early.
The pit is covered with earth, and nobody plants there this year.
The last burning stops at the field wall. What grew is cut early and counted twice.
The rot is out. The ground will be sown again, and watched.

coldsnap.begin: The cold comes early and hard - the Ford freezes over in a night.
during: Firewood costs what wine cost last week, and the queue for it is longer.
The Watch walk in pairs now, because one man alone stops moving.
The Ford is a road now, and nobody trusts it enough to use it.
The forge is the warmest room in Bellmire, and the smith charges for the privilege.
Water freezes in the bucket between the well and the door.
Caravans turn back at the hill, and the market has empty boards.
They bring the lambs indoors and share the floor with them.
The chapel takes in whoever has no fire, and the chapel is full.
Nails of ice hang off every eave, long enough to be dangerous.
The well head is thawed each morning with a kettle.
One oven bakes for the whole street, to save the wood.
The garrison drills indoors and complains, which keeps it warm.
Cattle breath stands in the byre like smoke that will not leave.
Two nights running, nobody goes further than the next door.
The river takes a skin of ice and the ferry stops for the first time in years.
Firewood doubles in price by noon and the Watch stands over the woodpile.
The old and the young are moved into the Keep hall together.
Livestock is brought indoors and lives among the household.
Building stops: the mortar will not set and nobody pretends it will.
The Ford is ice, so the trade is ice too - nothing moves either way.
Firewood is rationed and the rationing is read out by the crier.
The wells are broken open with a mallet each morning.
Work in Craft Row halts; the forge is the warmest room in Bellmire.
The chapel is full because the chapel is heated.
Breath smokes in the market; the stalls sell hot cider and nothing else.
The smiths run the forges all night, not for work but for warmth.
The pump is frozen. Snow is melted for the soup.
Sheep are brought into the houses. Nobody complains.
The Watch walks double shifts in every cloak it owns.
Frost cracks the water-barrels one by one, like slow thunder.
The pump is frozen solid, and the well-rope is stiff as a bar.
Breath hangs in the air like small ghosts.
Ice on the inside of the shutters; the hearth gets all the love.
A lamb is carried inside, wrapped in a good coat.
The Ford is a pale road, and the carters test it with a pole and a prayer.
The stew freezes between pot and bowl, and the cook weeps.
Ice on the inside of the shutters, and the children breathe clouds at the table.
The well-rope freezes and the Watch break it with a mallet.
Sheep are brought into the hall, and the hall smells of sheep.
Frost on every beard in the tavern, and no one takes his coat off.
The water bucket has a lid of ice by morning, and the lid is thick.
Frost on the inside of the shutters. The fire is not enough.
The ford-ice sings in the night, long and low, and then it is quiet.
Fires are banked high and the neighbours sleep three to a room.
The Watch stamps on the bridge in the dark and counts doors with smoke at the chimney.
coldsnap.pass: The thaw comes. The Ford runs again, and Bellmire counts who it kept.
coldsnap.cost: Livestock lost and work stopped: building, trade and the fields all halt until the thaw.
begin_alt: The cold comes early and hard, and the Ford freezes over in a night.
Winter arrives a month ahead of schedule and makes itself at home.
Ice on the inside of the shutters by morning. This will be a bad one.
The Ford freezes in a night, and the cold is not finished.
Winter comes early and hard, and the firewood price rises with the sun.
Cold enough by dusk that the ground rings underfoot.
The cold arrives overnight and takes the fen's water with it.
Frost on the inside of the shutters by morning - this one means to stay.
The cold arrives early and hard, and the Ford freezes in a night.
Ice on the inside of the shutters by morning.
The river stops moving. So does most of Bellmire.
A cold out of the high country that stops work where it finds it.
The Ford is ice thick enough to walk and too thin to trust.
The frost comes down before the harvest is fully in.
Cold enough that the mortar will not set and the masons go home.
The wells skin over. The firewood is counted like grain.
Frost in the first week of harvest. The pond goes solid and the pump-handle sticks to the hand.
The cold drops out of a clear sky. By dawn the Ford is glass.
Breath hangs in the air. The cattle bunch in the barns and will not be moved.
A hard frost comes a month early and finds every field still standing.
Ice on the trough, ice on the latch, ice in the beard. The cold came with no warning.
The wind swings north and the temperature falls off a cliff.
Frost writes on every window in a single night, and the river stops mid-sentence.
The cold arrives early, uninvited, with its boots on the table.
The crier announces a cold of the sort that has names, and none of them polite.
The first frost comes early and does not leave.
A wind from the north with teeth in it. The pond is hard by evening.
Every puddle is glass at dawn, and the geese leave in the night.
Ice on the inside of the glass. The Ford rings like a plate when a boot comes down.
The cold arrives overnight and the water-butts crack with a sound like a shot.
pass_alt: The thaw comes. The Ford runs, and Bellmire counts who it kept.
The ice gives up. Water moves again, and so does the town.
The cold breaks. The first cart over the Ford gets a cheer it did not expect.
The ice on the Ford breaks up and goes downriver in plates.
The thaw arrives. The eaves drip all day and nobody minds the mud.
It warms. The chapel empties, and the fires go out one at a time.
The thaw comes. The town counts who came through, and how much wood is left.
It breaks, and the river runs again. Nobody cheers; it is too early for that.
The thaw. Water moves in the river and the Ford is a ford again.
The cold lets go. The scaffolds fill up with masons by noon.
Ice off the river, mud in the lanes, and everybody glad of the mud.
The frost breaks. The building starts where it stopped.
Warm wind off the water. The town stretches and gets back to it.
The thaw comes. The lost livestock is counted and the rest turned out.
The river runs. The traders come down it the same day.
Over. The firewood that is left is stacked for next time.
The ice cracks and the Ford groans and runs. Bellmire thaws and takes the count.
The wind comes round to the south. Icicles drip, and then fall.
The cold lets go. Firewood is cheap again by week's end.
The frost breaks. The town unbundles itself and goes back out to work.
A grey thaw. Mud, meltwater, and the long list of who did not make it.
The snap ends. The Ford runs, and the ferryman wants his pole back.
Icicles drip. A drip, then a trickle, then the sweetest sound in the valley.
The Ford groans, cracks, and runs again; the carters cheer.
The sun comes out and warms the thatch, and the town sheds its coats one by one.
The ice cracks on the river like a shot. The thaw has come, late and welcome.
Eaves drip. For the first time in days, nobody is at the woodpile.
The Ford runs again. Bellmire counts who it lost to the cold.
The ice goes out of the Ford with a long groan. Bellmire takes off its second coat.
The cold lets go. The carters are on the road before the sun is.

Additive; dead until wired.
disasters._note_variants_c47: Widened C-cycle 47: flood, blight and coldsnap begin_alt 16 -> 22, pass_alt 16 -> 22, during 24 -> 30, matching the other seven disasters. begin, pass and cost are UNCHANGED. Additive; dead until wired.
disasters._note_variants_c56: C-56: +6 during, +3 begin_alt, +3 pass_alt per disaster across 13 disasters (156 lines). Same shapes; 'cost' statements untouched (the build worker reads those).
disasters._note_variants_c69: C-69: +4 during, +3 begin_alt, +3 pass_alt per disaster across 13 disasters (130 lines). Same shapes; cost statements untouched (the build worker reads those). Dead until wired.
disasters._note_variants_c148: C-148: +3 during lines on each of the 13 disasters (39 lines). Every disaster's during array is now 43. No mechanics, no cost statements touched. _note_ key: expected zero-hit, wire nothing.

events._note: Random world events (D33): bandit and monster camps that stand until cleared, and a wandering boss scaled to the town's level. Dead until wired.
events._note_variants: Added C-cycle 11: 3 more bandit camps (4 -> 7), 3 more monster camps (3 -> 6) in the same key shape, and appears_alt / while_alt / cleared_alt on wandering_boss - there is only one wandering boss, so its three lines would otherwise repeat verbatim every time it walks. Additive; dead until wired.

bandit_camps.name: The Gallows Oak
bandit_camps.appears: Red Harl's lot have taken the west road. No caravan reaches the Ford unbled.
bandit_camps.while: Trade caravans are robbed; the market runs short and prices climb.
bandit_camps.cleared: Red Harl hangs from his own Gallows Oak. The west road is open again.
appears_alt: Red Harl is back under the Gallows Oak, and the west road has gone quiet the wrong way.
The west road has a toll again, and Red Harl set it. No caravan reaches the Ford unbled.
There are new ropes on the Gallows Oak. Red Harl's lot hold the west road.
A caravan came in short a driver and a wheel. Red Harl holds the west road.
Red Harl has hung a new rope on the Gallows Oak, and the west road pays for the length of it.
Red Harl has hung fresh rope on the Gallows Oak. The west road is his again.
A driver reached the Ford with one wheel and no cargo. Red Harl is on the west road.
while_alt: Caravans come in robbed or not at all; the market runs short and the prices climb.
Every west-road caravan is bled. Stalls go empty and what is left costs more.
Trade bleeds on the west road - short stock in the market, and a higher price on all of it.
The caravans pay Red Harl first. The market pays for it in empty shelves and dear goods.
The west-road caravans are robbed; the market thins and prices climb.
The west road is shut to honest carts; the market runs thin and prices climb.
Caravans are stripped on the west road; the stalls empty and the prices rise.
cleared_alt: Red Harl hangs from his own oak. The west road carries caravans, not corpses.
The Gallows Oak earns its name. The west road is open.
Red Harl's lot are scattered off the west road. The next caravan comes in whole.
The oak is used properly at last. Trade runs the west road again.
Red Harl swings from the oak he was so proud of. The west road runs.
Red Harl's rope is cut down and the Oak is only a tree. The west road opens.
The Gallows Oak is cleared. The caravans come in with their loads, and their drivers.

bandit_camps.name: The Mire Nest
bandit_camps.appears: Sedge the Toll holds the fen path and taxes everyone who is not her.
bandit_camps.while: Every trader by the fen pays Sedge first; the town's cut shrinks.
bandit_camps.cleared: Sedge the Toll pays her own toll at last. The fen path clears.
appears_alt: Sedge the Toll is back on the fen path, and she still taxes everyone who is not her.
There is a rope across the fen path and Sedge the Toll holding the end of it.
The fen path has a tollkeeper nobody appointed. Sedge is in the Mire Nest again.
Traders come in light and say the same name: Sedge the Toll.
Sedge the Toll has put stakes in the fen path and a price on every one.
Sedge the Toll is back on the fen path with her hand out.
The fen path has a gate on it now, and Sedge keeps the key.
while_alt: Every trader by the fen pays Sedge before he pays Bellmire; the town's cut shrinks.
The fen trade is taxed twice. Sedge takes hers first and the town takes what is left.
Sedge's toll comes off the top of every fen crossing; the town's share thins by the day.
What the fen path earns, Sedge earns. The town's cut falls while the Nest stands.
The fen traders pay Sedge before they pay Bellmire; the town's cut thins.
Fen traders pay Sedge first and Bellmire after; the town's cut shrinks.
Sedge takes her share at the fen path, and the town's cut shrinks to match.
cleared_alt: Sedge the Toll pays her own toll. The fen path is free.
The Mire Nest is pulled apart. Nobody is charging for the fen now.
Sedge's rope comes down off the fen path. So does Sedge.
The fen path is honest again. The town's cut comes back whole.
Sedge the Toll is dragged out of the reeds. The fen path is free to walk.
The Mire Nest is emptied. Sedge the Toll pays at last, and the fen path is free.
The fen gate is down and Sedge with it. Traders pay the town and no one else.

bandit_camps.name: The Burnt Mill
bandit_camps.appears: Cob Ashfoot's raiders have holed up in the burnt mill, firing a field a night to keep the town afraid.
bandit_camps.while: A field burns most nights; harvest and morale both drop.
bandit_camps.cleared: The Burnt Mill burns one last time. Cob Ashfoot runs, and keeps running.
appears_alt: Smoke off the burnt mill again. Cob Ashfoot is firing a field a night to keep the town afraid.
Cob Ashfoot is back in the burnt mill, and the sky over the fields is orange by midnight.
A field went up in the dark and nobody lit it. Cob Ashfoot holds the mill.
The burnt mill has lights in it. Cob Ashfoot's raiders are in residence.
There is smoke over the burnt mill again. Cob Ashfoot has found his flint.
Cob Ashfoot is in the Burnt Mill again, and the sky to the east is orange.
A field is alight east of town. Cob Ashfoot's raiders are back in the mill.
while_alt: A field burns most nights; the harvest comes in short and the town sleeps badly.
Another field a night. Harvest drops, and so does every face in the market.
The fields burn by turns - less grain at the measure and less heart in the town.
Cob takes a field a night. Harvest and morale both go with it.
A field goes up most nights; the harvest suffers, and so does the mood.
Another field goes up after dark; the harvest falls and the town does not rest.
A field burns most nights; the crop falls short and spirits fall with it.
cleared_alt: The burnt mill burns one last time. Cob Ashfoot runs and keeps running.
Cob Ashfoot is out of the mill and out of the valley. The fields keep their fire to the hearth.
The mill is ash and the fields are not. Cob Ashfoot is gone.
No lights in the burnt mill tonight. The harvest comes in whole.
The mill is put out for good. Cob Ashfoot runs, and does not look back at the glow.
The Burnt Mill is taken. Cob Ashfoot is last seen running through his own smoke.
The mill is cold and empty. No more fields burn.

bandit_camps.name: Scarside Camp
bandit_camps.appears: The Weasel's crew squat at the scar's edge, robbing the delvers who climb out.
bandit_camps.while: Returning delvers are waylaid; their gold and loot never reach Bellmire.
bandit_camps.cleared: Scarside Camp is cleared. Delvers come up to friends now, not knives.
appears_alt: The Weasel's crew are at the scar's edge again, robbing whoever climbs out.
Scarside Camp is up. The Weasel waits where the delvers surface.
A delver came up rich and walked in poor. The Weasel holds the scar's edge.
There are knives at the lip of the scar, and The Weasel counting behind them.
The Weasel has dug a crew in beside the scar and lies in wait for whoever climbs out.
The Weasel is camped at the scar's lip again, waiting for whoever climbs out.
Delvers who climbed out last night did not reach town. The Weasel is at the scar.
while_alt: Delvers are waylaid coming up; their gold and loot never reach Bellmire.
Every climb out is taxed in blood. What the scar gives, Scarside Camp keeps.
The Weasel takes it at the lip - the delve pays and the town sees none of it.
Loot stops at the scar's edge. Nothing a delver earns gets as far as the gate.
Delvers coming home are waylaid; their gold and loot never reach Bellmire.
Climbing delvers are robbed at the scar's edge; their gold and loot never reach Bellmire.
The Weasel's crew take what delvers carry up, and Bellmire sees none of it.
cleared_alt: Scarside Camp is cleared. Delvers come up to friends now, not knives.
The Weasel is pulled off the scar's edge. The climb out is safe.
Nothing waits at the lip but daylight. Scarside Camp is finished.
The Weasel runs out of patience and throat. Loot reaches the gate again.
The Weasel's burrow is dug out. The scar's edge is safe to walk.
The Weasel is run off the scar's lip. Delvers climb out to the Watch.
Scarside Camp is cleared, and the loot comes home with the people carrying it.

bandit_camps.name: The Drover's Rest
bandit_camps.appears: Juno Blackhand has taken the drovers' inn on the north road and left the sign hanging.
bandit_camps.while: Livestock driven to market never arrive; the pens stand empty on market day.
bandit_camps.cleared: The Drover's Rest changes hands again. Juno Blackhand does not leave with it.
appears_alt: Juno Blackhand holds the drovers' inn on the north road, and left the sign hanging.
The Drover's Rest has new keepers. Juno Blackhand took it with the beer still in the cask.
No drover has come down the north road in days. Juno Blackhand is why.
There is smoke from the Drover's Rest and nobody paying for a bed. Juno Blackhand is in.
The sign still says Drover's Rest. The door says Juno Blackhand.
The sign still hangs at the Drover's Rest. Juno Blackhand is the one inside.
No drovers have come down the north road in days. Juno Blackhand has the inn.
while_alt: Livestock driven to market never arrive; the pens stand empty on market day.
The herds go up the north road and stop there. Market day opens to bare pens.
Juno takes the beasts before the town sees them - empty pens, and no meat at the measure.
Nothing on four legs gets past the Rest. The market pens hold air.
Livestock bound for market never arrives; the pens stand empty on market day.
Herds are turned off at the Rest; the pens stand empty on market day.
Livestock bound for market never come down the north road; the pens are bare.
cleared_alt: The Drover's Rest changes hands again. Juno Blackhand does not leave with it.
Juno Blackhand is taken out of the Rest. The herds come down the north road.
The sign still hangs. The man who hung it does too.
The Drover's Rest serves drovers. The pens fill by market day.
The Rest is retaken and the sign rehung. Juno Blackhand gets a room with bars on the window.
Juno Blackhand is carried out of the Drover's Rest. The drovers take the rooms back.
The Rest has a landlord again, and the herds come down the north road.

bandit_camps.name: The Quarry Camp
