The beam swings and settles. Nobody is being measured.
Whatever he took off the top, you have again.
Murkspit is down. Stand up to your full height.
The strickle lies flat on the floor. Straight, and still.
The pans hang level, for once.
The measure tips. Grain goes everywhere.
A last sway of the beam, and it stops.

arrive: Something back there just marked one of you.
Three cloths hang to dry. The vat is steaming.
The dye-house floor is wet to the ankle, and the wet is not water.
A man at a vat, paddle in hand, blue to the elbow.
Woad, madder, weld. He has all three going.
The vat is full. He has a use for it.
He lifts the cloth out and looks at it. Then he looks at you.
Every sheet on the frame is a different colour. None of them are finished.
Venomshade has chosen someone.
fall: Venomshade is down. The vat goes on steaming.
The paddle slides out of the dye and lies across the rim.
The cloths hang as they were. Nobody is marked.
Blue to the elbow, and still. The fire under the vat burns low.
Venomshade is down. The stain stays where it is.
A last drip from the hem of a sheet.
The vat is cooling. The colour does not fade.
He had a colour for everyone. It was not enough.

arrive: Your edge came back green.
Copper plates stacked over a pan of vinegar. The air stings.
A man green to the elbow, and green to the neck besides.
He has a scraper in one hand. He is in no hurry.
A brazier on legs, and a rack of plates curing above it.
Whatever you hit him with, he will give it back worse.
He has done this twenty years. The green does not wash off.
The sword on the floor is green to the hilt. It was somebody's.
Verdigris. It gets into everything he touches, and he touches iron.
fall: Corrodan is down. The plates go on curing.
The scraper slips out of his hand and lies on the floor.
Green to the elbow, and still. The brazier burns low.
A curl of scraped green drops off the blade. Nobody picks it up.
Corrodan is down. The sting goes out of the air.
Your iron is yours again. It will want a good cleaning.
The vinegar is cooling. The plates stay as they are.
He made his living from what rust and copper do. Now it is done.

arrive: It took a copy of one of you.
A flask of sand on the floor, and a crucible hung over it.
The sand is pressed into the shape of somebody. Somebody in here.
He pours without looking up. He has poured a good many.
The pour is red, and it is the only light in the room.
A row of castings hangs on pegs along the box. None of them are finished.
The mould is warm. Someone has been using it all morning.
He taps the box with a rammer, twice, the way you check a loaf.
Whatever he makes, he makes to order. Today's order is you.
fall: Ashform is down. The pour runs out across the sand.
The crucible tips and empties. The sand drinks it.
The copy stands a moment longer than he does. Then it does not.
The box cracks along its seam. Nothing comes out of it.
The rammer drops. Nobody is making your likeness now.
A cast, half set, on the floor. It has your reach. It does not move.
Ashform is down. The room cools by degrees.
The last pour went on the floor.

arrive: Paid by the tail.
A willow cage on his hip. Five tails hang in it already.
He counts what is in the cage before he looks at you.
A long pole with an iron butt, and a lamp held over the tally.
Whatever else dies in here goes in his cage. He keeps count.
He is not here for you. He is here for what you leave behind.
The cage has twelve bays. He is in no hurry to fill them.
Rats, mostly. It has been a good season.
Leave the small ones standing. He goes hungry in an empty room.
fall: Skivven is down. The cage hits the floor.
The tally lamp gutters. Nobody is counting now.
The pole rolls off across the flags.
The willow splits at the lashings. Out it all comes.
He kept a good tally. It is over.
Skivven is down. The room is quiet for the first time.
One more tail for the cage, and nobody left to be paid for it.
Paid up. The lamp goes out last.

arrive: He puts a yoke on one of you.
An ash beam across his shoulders, and two iron bows hanging off it.
One bow hangs open. That is not an accident.
He talks to nobody. He drives.
A chain coiled at his feet, link through link.
A goad in his fist, cut this week. Everything else on him is old.
The collar clicks shut on one of you. The chain goes tight.
He has driven oxen forty years. You are not the first team.
Hit him, and the one in the collar pays half.
fall: Yokebane is down. The chain goes slack.
The collar falls open and rings on the floor.
He drops the goad. He does not look at it.
The yoke comes off the beam, and it is only iron.
Cut the chain and the yoke comes free. Now nobody wears it.
The ash beam rolls off his shoulders and lies still.
Yokebane is down. The team is your own again.
Both bows hang empty.

arrive: A board stands up out of the dark, on a pole.
It keeps its face to you. Whichever of you it is.
A pavise, taller than a man, hung on a post.
Hit the board and nothing happens. Go round it.
He crouches behind it. A spear rests along the top edge.
The board swings to whoever is hurting him most.
Plank, hide and iron straps. Mended where it split.
Two of you, then. One to hold his eye, one to go round.
He does not step out. He turns the board.
fall: Shieldmaw is down. The board is only a board.
The post gives. The pavise leans and lies flat.
The spear slides off the top edge and rattles.
Nothing swings round now.
The hinge post stands empty.
He kept his face to you to the last.
Shieldmaw is down. Someone got round.
Plank and hide on the floor, and nobody behind them.

arrive: Five small lights low over the fen. None of them are lamps.
A man on boards, in a hood with no eyeholes.
Something out there is listening.
He walks the boards without a sound. He carries a pole.
The hood is sewn shut. He does not need to see you.
Stand still and he does not know you are here.
He comes for whoever moved last.
Swing, step or drink. Whoever does it, he turns that way.
Five lights hang off him, and the fog sits round each one.
fall: Bogwarden is down. The lights go out one at a time.
The pole drops across the boards.
The fen is quiet. It was not, before.
He kept his head turned to whoever moved. Now no one has to keep still.
Five lights on the floor, and all of them cold.
Bogwarden is down. You may move.
The hood falls open. There was nothing to see.
The boards creak once and are still.

arrive: A stand of sugar, taller than a man, and the smell of burnt honey.
Nothing you carry will mark it. Not steel, not flame.
It holds out a comfit. Small, bright, polite.
Take the sweet and you can cut it. That is the offer.
The comfit cuts where steel will not. It is only sugar.
Whoever holds one swings slow. The sugar gums the hand.
It has more sweets than you have hands. It does not hurry.
A pair of nippers, and a stand hung with comfits. Somebody made these by hand.
It hands one to the nearest of you, and waits.
fall: Brindle is down. The stand comes apart in tiers.
The shell was sugar all the way through.
The nippers drop. The comfits roll off across the floor.
Your hand is sticky yet. It will pass.
Nothing left to hand round.
Brindle is down. The sweet was the only way in.
Sugar crunches underfoot, and the smell of honey goes thin.
The tray is empty. It gave you all it had.

arrive: A stooped man in a linen coif, bent over a brass basin.
He holds a fleam over the rim. He is in no hurry.
Five cupping horns hang at his thigh, worn smooth.
Nobody mends in here. What you spend, the basin takes.
Whatever you heal goes into the basin. He drinks from it.
The level in the basin is the mending you paid for.
Tip the basin and your own healing comes back.
His gown is undyed wool, washed grey. An old trade, long practised.
He has seen a great many wounds. He keeps them open.
fall: Gulworth is down. The basin goes over and runs across the floor.
The fleam drops. It rings once on the stone.
Mending comes back. Wounds close as they should.
He bent over the bowl to the last.
The basin is empty. It held more than he took from you.
Gulworth is down. Heal what you like.
The coif is spotted dark. None of it is his.
The horns swing on their cord and are still.

arrive: A tall man in a parish coat, a staff in one hand and a board held up over his head.
It says who speaks, and it is not you.
Four brass pegs on the board. Each is a call he has left.
He names one of you. Then he names the same one again.
The rest hold and watch. You do not choose who acts.
Count the pegs from the door. When they are gone, he is spent.
Knock the board off his arm and the order is yours again.
The coat has been to every moot for years. The staff and the board are his office, and he keeps them.
He stands a head above the people he calls. He has never been argued with.
act: He calls {name}. Again.
{name}, once more. The rest hold.
A peg turns down. It is {name} still.
The staff comes down. {name} acts. Nobody else.
Same name, same call. The rest watch.
You were not asked.
One peg spent. {name} is called again.
broken: The board is off his arm. The order is yours.
Brass pegs bounce on the stone. Choose for yourselves.
The board cracks across. He has no call left to make.
The staff stays up and the board goes down. Act as you like.
fall: Ordrik is down. The board hits the floor and the pegs scatter.
The staff rolls clear. Nobody is calling now.
The order comes back to you. Act as you like.
He kept the call to the last peg.
The board lies face down. It has nothing left to say.
Ordrik is down. Whoever stood watching can move.
Brass pegs on the stone. Somebody counts them out of habit.
The coat is creased where the board rode. He held it a long time.

arrive: Three timber legs and a frame between them. Something is being driven into the floor.
A bruised pile stands out of the stone. Over it, an iron monkey hangs under the head.
A hauler leans back on the fall-rope, off to one side. He is not the danger. He is the reason it is loaded.
Hear the haul. Slow, a rope paying through a block. Each pull is a step nearer the top.
Then the hold. That is the whole warning. Nothing moves and everything waits.
Stand off the pile for the drop. Come back in while it hauls.
Whatever is on the pile when the monkey falls is finished.
The timber is river-soaked and bruised. The rope is frayed. The iron is the one sound thing here.
A working man keeps his monkey. He keeps it better than himself.
act: The haul. Slow. The rope runs.
Pull, and pull. The iron climbs.
It hangs at the top. Nobody breathes.
The hold. Get off the pile.
The rope lets go.
It comes down on the count.
broken: The rope parts. The monkey stays where it fell.
A leg splits and the frame sits down crooked. It cannot haul.
The head block cracks. The iron has nowhere to go up.
The hauler lets the rope run through his hands and does not take it up again.
fall: Breachar is down. The monkey lies on the pile and does not rise.
The rope goes slack and falls in a heap.
Nothing is hauling now. Nothing is held. Walk the floor.
It dropped on the count to the last.
The frame leans on one leg and holds no weight.
Breachar is down. The pile is a stump with a dent in its head.
The hauler sits on the wet stone and looks at his hands. Nobody asks him anything.
The iron is sound. The timber round it is not.

arrive: A long trough on trestles, and the cloth in it heaped over the rim. Two timber hammers hang above.
A man stands off to the left, one hand on the bar. His apron is wet to the knee.
Something is being worked here. The cloth is pale and thick and new off the loom.
The stocks lift and fall. Each fall presses the cloth down. It comes back up.
The trough is full. Watch the cloth, not the man.
Every blow you land goes into the cloth. It keeps them. It gives them all back at once.
Stop hitting it. Break the stocks. Or wring it early and take a small one.
His wool is worn through at the elbow. The goods in the trough are this week's, and clean.
A working man's stock is better kept than he is.
act: The stocks lift. The cloth settles.
The cloth swells. It is rising over the rim.
Water runs off the lip and darkens the floor.
The man leans on the bar. The trough shudders.
It is full. It cannot hold more.
The wring. Get out from under it.
broken: A stock splits at the pin and hangs. It does not fall true.
The bar slips from his hand. The hammers stop where they are.
The cloth tears at the rim and the water goes out across the floor, a small flood and no more.
The trough cracks along the seam. It will not hold a load.
fall: Wrynn is down. The hammers hang still.
The cloth sags in the trough and gives up its water slowly.
Nothing is wringing. Nothing is full. Walk the floor.
It was empty at the end. You stopped in time, or you paid for it.
The man sits on the bar and wrings his cap between his hands.
Wrynn is down. The cloth is the only good thing left in the room.
He lifts a fold of the stock and looks at it, then lays it back.
The trough drips. That is the last sound it makes.

arrive: A stack of this year's sheaves, three courses high, and a man standing on the top of it.
Count the courses. Three. The bottom band is split open and sheaves have spilled out across the floor.
A pole ladder leans on the back of the stack. A rake lies across the top. The man holds a long fork.
His smock is blue and thin and patched at the shoulder. The straw under him is cut this week, and gold.
Hit him and he pitches a fresh sheaf under his boots. He climbs a course.
Count again after every blow. Each course is one blow's worth of height.
Up there nothing with a hand on it can reach him. He pitches down at you for nothing.
Cut the bottom course out from under him. Or bring something with reach.
A field hand at the end of a harvest keeps his crop better than his coat.
act: A sheaf goes under his feet. One course higher.
The stack grows. Count it.
The fork comes down from above.
He is past your reach. Hands will not do it now.
The third course. There is nowhere higher to go.
He stoops, and pitches. Stand clear of the line.
broken: The bottom band parts. The course slumps and the whole stack sits down a step.
A course is cut out from under him. He drops, and catches the fork to keep his feet.
The withy gives at the base and sheaves run out across the floor.
The ladder slides from the back of the stack and lies flat. He has nothing to climb.
fall: Huskpile is down. The stack is a heap of straw.
The fork stands in the floor where it landed.
Nothing is climbing now. Nothing is out of reach. Walk the floor.
He came down course by course. You hurt him slowly, or you did not hurt him at all.
The rake lies in the straw. He does not look for it.
Huskpile is down. The straw is the only good thing in the room.
He sits on the spilled sheaves and picks a stalk out of his sleeve. Nobody asks him anything.
The straw is sweet and new-cut. It settles, and the room goes quiet.

arrive: A mason on a plank, a hod on his shoulder, and a bare place in the room where a wall ought to go.
The hod is full of blocks. Count them. Each one is a course he has not laid yet.
The last wall in here is new. The lime is pale and wet and still has the trowel marks in it.
His smock is white to the elbow and gone through at the cuff. The lime on the wall behind him is this morning's.
Hit him and he turns and lays a course. It goes up across the room, and the room is smaller.
The wet course gives to any hand. Break it now or do not bother.
Leave it a while and it sets. Nothing you carry will open set stone.
Swing at the man, or swing at his wall. The same blow will not do both.
A bricklayer who is paid by the course keeps his tools cleaner than his coat.
fall: Wetwall is down. The trowel lies in the lime where it fell.
The hod tips and the last blocks roll out across the floor.
Nothing is laying up now. Nothing is closing. Walk the floor.
The walls he laid stand where they are. The soft ones you broke, and the hard ones you did not.
He sits on the plank and scrapes his trowel on the edge of the hod. Nobody asks him anything.
Wetwall is down. The new lime is the only good thing in the room.
The plumb line hangs straight, and nothing is out of true but the floor.
The lime smells clean and sharp. It goes pale as it dries, and the room is quiet.

arrive: A customs man at a bench, a press in his two hands, and a strip of lead blanks on his hip.
Count the blanks. Each one is a pack he can still shut.
He does not shout. He stamps. Whoever is bitten has a pack that will not open.
The pack is not taken. Everything is still in it. It is only not yours.
Flask, bandage, scroll. Whatever the hero walked in with stays shut while Leadbite stands.
The press is oiled. The coat is not. He has kept the one thing he is paid for.
The seal is warm, and the lead is soft and bright where it bit.
Win on what is already in your hands, or break the press.
The room smells of lamp oil and cold lead. Somebody is keeping tally.
fall: Leadbite is down. The press lies open on the bench.
The strip on his hip is still full. Nobody counts it.
The seals come off the packs the way wax comes off a letter. Pull the strap and it opens.
Everything the hero had is where it was. It is theirs again.
He sits with his back to the bench and wipes the screw with his sleeve. He does it carefully.
Leadbite is down. The lead is the only bright thing in the room.
The bench is clean, the ledger is closed, and nobody is owed a fee.
Open the pack. Take a breath. Walk the floor.

arrive: A cooper with a cask raised in both hands and a post on his back, hung with iron hoops.
Count the hoops on the post. Each one is another of you he can shut in.
He does not shout. He sets the cask down over one hero and drives the hoops home with a mallet.
The hero is not out of the fight. They keep swinging, blind, from inside the staves.
No bandage reaches them, no brew, no shout, no shield. The line can see them and cannot touch them.
The mallet is oiled. The apron is wet through and has not been washed.
Break the staves and get one of your own back, or hit the cooper while one of you fights alone in the dark.
The cask is new, and the wood is pale where the adze went through it.
The cellar smells of damp oak and cold iron. Somebody is keeping tally.
fall: Hoopfast is down. The mallet lies on the cask.
The hoops on the post stop ringing. Nobody counts the ones that are left.
The staves come away the way a loose cask comes apart. Whoever was inside walks out.
Everyone is on their feet again, and the line can reach them.
He sits on the upturned cask and wipes the mallet head with his apron. He does it slowly.
Hoopfast is down. The new oak is the only pale thing in the cellar.
The cellar is quiet, and every hoop is where he left it.
Knock the staves down. Draw a breath. Walk the floor.

arrive: A sentry in a kettle hat with his back to a gate winch, a lamp on the drum head, and a ratchet plate at his foot.
Count the notches in the plate. Four. The dog sits in one of them.
He does not shout. He heaves the capstan a quarter turn, and the whole line comes round one place.
Your front rank is at the back and your back rank is at the front. Nobody is hurt. Nobody is gone.
Every reach, every guard, every heal was lined up on a body that is no longer standing there.
The bars are greased and the lamp is cold and blue. He has the look of a man who has stood this watch before.
Jam the dog in the ratchet plate and the turn stops. It costs you a turn on the floor and not on the thing hitting you.
The drum is pale oak, scrubbed white. The iron is the darkest thing in the room.
The guardroom smells of lamp oil and cold mail. Somebody has come to relieve the watch.
fall: Watchturn is down. The bars hang slack in the drum.
The dog drops into its notch and the capstan does not move again.
The line settles where it stands. Front is front. Back is back.
The lamp on the drum head goes out. Nobody lights it.
He sits against the winch with his kettle hat in his lap. He does it quietly.
Watchturn is down. The drum is the only pale thing in the room.
The plate is quiet, and every notch is empty but the one.
Take your places. Draw a breath. Walk the floor.

arrive: Someone is rubbing a name off the wall.
A man in a dark coat at the foot of a pale slab, a stone in both hands, a heap of grit at his boots.
He does not block and he does not heal. He waits for the round to end, then draws the stone down the slab.
Whatever you did last comes off. The blow lifts, the wound opens, the guard is gone.
Do your real work early. Spend your last action on something you can stand to lose.
Hitting harder does nothing. The hit is the thing he takes back.
Count the cuts on the plinth. Five on every face. Each one is another round he can wipe.
The slab is cut with names in rows, and the ends of the rows are ragged. The grit on the floor is fresh.
A dust mask, a hood, and two cold eyes under it. The crypt is quiet. He has all the time there is.
fall: Scourstone is down. The stone lies where it fell, and the slab keeps what is on it.
The names stay cut. Nobody rubs them out now.
The heap of grit stops growing.
He folds over the plinth with his mask still on. He goes down slowly and does not make a sound.
Whatever you do now stays done.
Count the cuts on the plinth again. Nothing was taken from any of them.
The three spare slates slide off his back and lie flat on the floor.
Take your places. Draw a breath. Walk the floor.

arrive: A flat-bottomed boat is being poled up the passage.
A man in stiff grey sacking stands in a black punt, a pale pole in his hands. The water under it is only a wet floor.
The punt holds one. He takes one of you aboard, and only that one can hurt him.
Nobody else's blows land. They go through him like wind through a net.
He chooses. If you stacked everything on one hero, watch that hero stand on the bank.
Look along the gunwales. Pale pegs, one for every crossing he has left.
The rest of you are not idle. Draw the pegs. Shift the fare.
A plank for a seat, and one pale seat only. A boot sits on it, left behind by the last passenger.
He does not hurry and he does not speak. The river never asked anyone twice.
fall: Slackwater is down. The pole floats off on its own, and the punt rides low and empty.
The last peg is drawn. He has to put the one he holds down, and nobody is left to take.
Everyone's blows land now. Nobody waits their turn on the bank.
The punt turns slowly against the wall and stays there.
The grey sacking sags in the boat. There is silt in the folds.
Count the seats. There is one. It is empty.
Water drains out of the passage the way it came in, without a sound.
Take your places. Wipe the pole. Walk the floor.

arrive: Something is taking a turn on a drum up ahead.
A low drum slung in a timber frame, wound with pale rope. A bowed man leans his whole weight on the bar.
He does not strike. He winds. Whoever a hook is in gets drawn back toward the door.
Nothing you did is undone. You are simply not where you were, and the blow you were about to land is out of reach.
Look at the floor. Three ropes lie across it, each with its own dark hook. Three is all he can have on at once.
A rope that is cut stays cut. Cut all three and the drum turns on nothing.
Hauling against him buys a yard. The next turn takes it back.
The iron pawl drops into the ratchet every tooth. The drum does not give a single turn back.
Greased iron, new hemp, a man in wool the colour of the timber. He has not stopped since you came in.
fall: Haulback is down. The bar swings loose and the drum runs out its last length of rope.
The last hook lies slack on the floor. Nobody is on it.
The pawl lifts out of the teeth and does not drop again.
He slides down the bar with both hands still on it.
Walk where you like. Nothing is drawing you back now.
Count the ropes. Three, and every one of them lying still.
The drum turns once more on its own weight, and stops.
Take your places. Coil the rope. Walk the floor.

arrive: Somebody is digging up ahead, and it is not for ore.
A man in a flat cap with a mattock, and a boarded ring in the floor at his feet. A ladder stands up out of it.
He does not swing at you. He digs. Whoever stands where he wants them not to be has no floor under them.
The delver is not hurt. They are simply at the bottom of a hole, and the next beat goes on the ladder.
He leaves the ladder every time. He is not a cruel man. He is a careful one.
The pit stays. When the fight moves on, the hole is still there.
Look at the room you came in by. It will not be the room you leave by.
Pale new timber shores the ring, and a dark heap of spoil sits behind him, still loose.
Clay to the knee, a clean flat cap, and not one wasted stroke. He has been at this since before you came in.
act: The mattock comes down. The floor goes from under {name}.
{name} is gone from the floor. A ladder is already standing in the hole.
He dug under {name} and not an inch to either side.
A new ring of boards, and {name} at the bottom of it.
One stroke and the stone goes soft. {name} drops a man's height.
The spoil heap grows by a barrow. {name} never saw him start.
Another hole, another ladder. {name} will want it.
broken: The haft is split. He is holding a stick.
The ladder is knocked out of the ring. He has nothing to dig with.
He sets the spade down and wipes his hands. The holes he dug stay open.
The mattock head rolls off the rim. No new ground opens, but mind the old.
fall: Underfoot is down. The mattock lies across the rim of the ring.
The ladder stands in its hole with nobody on it.
He sits down on the spoil heap with his hands open. He does not dig again.
The holes are still there. Mind where you put your feet.
A hole does not fill itself. Walk round them.
The room is not the room you came into. Count what is left of the floor.
One last shovelful slides off the heap and into the ring.
Take the ladders out. Board the holes. Walk the floor.

arrive: Somebody is standing in the way with a hand out.
A hooded man with a balance held up, and one flat palm.
He does not draw. He asks for a tenth of what this floor has paid you.
Pay it and he stands aside. No blow, no loss, the way is open.
Refuse and the hand closes. That is the worst thing on this floor.
Nobody drives him off. It is a debt, not a fight.
Look at the pans. One of them is waiting for your coin.
A dark satchel, a stooped back, a cowl with two pale eyes in it. He has stood here a long while.
The party settles it. The tenth, or the hand.
act: {name} counts out the tenth. The pan dips and he nods.
The balance comes level. {name} is quit of him.
{name} will not pay. The hand closes.
He weighs what {name} carries and names the tenth to the coin.
{name} puts a tenth on the pan. He does not thank anyone.
A tenth from {name}, and the way is open.
The balance tips against {name}. The hand comes out again.
broken: The beam is cracked. He cannot weigh what he is owed.
A cord parts and a pan drops. The count is lost.
The balance is on the floor. He holds out the hand anyway.
He looks at the broken scale and does not ask again.
fall: The balance hangs level. Nothing is owed.
The hand is open and empty. He is out of the way.
He steps aside and the way is clear.
The pans are still. Nobody owes him a coin.
Tenthpart has gone quiet. The tenth is settled.
He sets the balance down. The account is closed.
Whatever it cost, the floor is open again.
Count what you kept.

arrive: Something ahead is drawing the air in.
A broad man in pit wool, working a bellows backwards. A pale ribbed bag rides high on his back.
He does not strike anyone. He draws the room empty, a stroke at a time.
Every stroke, everybody in here acts a little slower. Whoever carries the most gives out first.
Look at the bag. It stands one band fuller every stroke. That is how long the room has left.
Nothing done to the man slows the count. Hit him all you like.
Three iron patches are stitched over the bag. It has been holed in those places before.
Hole the bag and the count stops.
Half-worn hide, newer iron on it, and a man who has not lost his rhythm since you came in.
act: The bellows draws. {name} is slower for it.
Another stroke. {name} feels the air go thin.
{name} is carrying the most, and it shows.
The bag stands a band fuller. {name} reaches for the next move and it comes late.
{name} breathes short. The bellows does not stop.
One stroke more. {name} is a half-beat behind.
{name} goes for the patch iron. The bag is a long way up his back.
broken: The bag is holed. The air stops moving.
A rent in the hide at the patch iron. The count stops where it stands.
He works the handles and nothing draws. The bag hangs slack.
The bellows wheeze. The room has stopped getting emptier.
fall: Deadair is down. The bellows hang slack in his hands.
The bag sags flat. The air comes back into the room.
Nobody is drawing on it now. Breathe.
The handles drop out of his grip and the count is gone.
He folds over the bag with his hands still on the bar.
Move how you like. Nothing is slowing you now.
The last stroke goes out of him and does not come back.
Take the bellows down. Mend the bag. Walk the floor.

arrive: Something ahead is turning, slow and even.
A tall man standing at a turnstile post, and a pale drum on the top of it behind him.
He does not chase anyone. He works the post, and the post works the room.
Land your best blow on him and you will be standing where he stood. He will be where you were.
He comes out of it beside whoever you were keeping back.
Nobody is taken and nobody is lost. Everybody is just somewhere else.
Look at the drum. It turns a third on every trade. Count the dark rungs.
The post turns only while nothing leans on it. A body set against it holds it.
Good wool, a clean plate under the post, and a man who has done this every day for years.
act: The post turns. {name} is standing where he stood.
{name} struck hardest and paid for it. The turnstile turns.
A third of a turn on the drum. {name} is somewhere new.
{name} comes out the far side of him, and the back rank has company.
He keeps to the turnstile. {name} keeps to the wrong place.
One more trade. {name} watches the drum, not the man.
{name} puts a shoulder to the post. It will not go round.
broken: A body against the post. Everything stops where it stands.
The turnstile will not turn. The drum stays on its rung.
He leans on the post and nothing gives. The trade is off.
The post is jammed. Everybody is where they chose to be.
fall: Evenhand is down. The drum hangs still.
The drum has stopped on its last rung.
He steps out of the turnstile and does not step back in.
The post is idle. Stand where you like.
Nobody trades with him now.
He lays a hand on the post and lets go of it.
The turnstile stands open. Nothing is owed.
Count who is beside you.

arrive: The air has gone thick. Something is seating a lid.
A man stood up through a wide flat ring at chest height. A cloth over his mouth, a lamp at his hip.
He does not come at anyone. He stands in the middle of the ring and screws it down.
Five pale pegs stand on the rim. One drops every notch.
When the last peg drops, the room is shut.
Every notch, everybody in here has a little less wind.
Nothing done to the room buys time back. Hit him all you like and the pegs still drop.
A shoulder under the ring and a lift will hold it. Whoever does that is not swinging.
Sound timber, kept iron, and pegs worn smooth where hands have been. He has done this before.
act: A peg drops. {name} takes a shorter breath.
The ring comes down a notch. {name} feels it in the chest.
{name} swings hard. The pegs do not care.
Another notch. {name} is winning on damage and losing on air.
{name} counts the pegs off the rim. There are fewer.
The lamp at his hip has gone small. {name} breathes through the pain of it.
One peg left standing. {name} is out of notches to spend.
broken: A shoulder under the ring. It holds where it stands.
The lid will not seat. A body is holding it up.
He leans on the haft and the ring does not go down. The pegs hold.
Nobody is swinging. The count stays where it is.
fall: Chokewell is down. The ring lies crooked on the floor.
The pegs still standing stay standing. Nothing drops.
The lid is off. The air comes back thin, then full.
He lets go of the haft. The ring rolls half a turn and lies flat.
Breathe. Slowly first.
He is out of the ring, and the ring is empty.
The lamp at his hip burns steady again.
Count the pegs still up. Be glad of each one.

arrive: Something ahead is taking up slack.
A man walking backward down a long lane, paying a rope out of his hands and taking it in again.
He does not strike anyone. He does not need to.
Three pale strands go into the frame behind him. One dark rope comes out the back.
Every notch, the hindmost of you is drawn a yard toward the middle.
When the last of you is inside one span, he lays the rope.
Then you are standing in one place, all of you. Whatever sweeps the room sweeps the lot.
Nothing done to him adds slack. Only a body walking out from the others does.
Plain hemp, a good worn frame, and a man who has walked this lane since before there was a town.
act: The strands draw in. {name} is a yard nearer the rest.
{name} takes a step back and the rope takes the step off him.
A notch. The party is a smaller shape than it was.
{name} was the hindmost. {name} is not any more.
He walks his backward walk. {name} finds a shoulder at each elbow.
The slack is nearly gone. {name} can count the boots in reach.
One span. {name} stands where everyone else stands.
broken: One of them walks out, away from the rest. The rope gives.
A delver steps wide. The strands go loose in his hands.
Slack. He has to walk back and take it up again.
Somebody chose to stand alone. It costs, and it holds.
fall: Drawtight is down. The rope lies in the grass in loops.
The strands go slack. Nothing draws.
Step apart. The lane is wide enough.
He lets the last of it run through his hands. It does not tighten.
The frame stands empty at the end of the lane.
Everybody has their own ground again. Use it.
The dark rope is only rope now.
Coil it or leave it. It will not pull.

arrive: Something ahead is holding a dish out.
A man standing square in the lane, a flat dark tray on one forearm and a sack at his hip.
He does not strike anyone. Nothing in the room is taken.
Each of you walks up and puts in. It is how the dole has always gone.
Three pieces of kit lie in the tray. Two more are already coming out of the sack's mouth.
He gives back, and it is not the same dealing.
Every swing in the party now comes off another trade's weight.
The sum of you is the same. Every one of you is in the wrong place in it.
Plain wool, an iron dish, a worn sack, and a patient face.
act: {name} swings and the weight is a stranger's.
The dish comes round. {name} is dealt a swing that was never theirs.
{name} reaches for the old stroke and it does not come.
Another turn of the dole. {name} stands in someone else's trade.
{name} hits like a different trade.
The dish is held out again. {name} puts in and is given back wrong.
Nobody is weaker. {name} is only holding the wrong end of the work.
broken: The dish goes down. The old swing comes back.
A delver knocks the tray aside. Every hand finds its own weight.
He stumbles and the dealing stops. Hands remember.
The dole is spoilt. It will have to start again.
fall: Dolehand is down. The dish rings on the floor.
The sack lies open. Nothing comes out of it.
Every swing is your own again.
Your hands know their own weight. Use it.
The dish is only iron now.
Dealt right again. Count the party and go on.
He hurt no one. Everyone is glad he is done.
Leave the sack. It has nothing more to give.

arrive: A low turning sound ahead, steady as a mill.
A closed iron drum on a frame, taller than a man, the crank at its side going round on its own.
Nobody is working it. It simply goes.
The wall is shut. Swing at it and the wall takes the blow and gives nothing back.
One opening in the drum, set on a slant. Every turn it swings past once.
A pale rim, a dark bowl, a few sugared lumps on the floor of it.
When the pan comes round, there is something to hit. Then it goes by again.
Hit the wall and you have spent your arm for nothing. Stand and wait, all of you.
Scoured bright iron. Sugar burns on to a dull pan, so someone keeps this one polished.
act: The pan comes round. {name} is ready for it.
{name} swings on the shut wall. Nothing marks it.
The mouth goes by and {name} is a beat late.
{name} holds the blow and counts the turn.
Round again. {name} looks at the opening and waits.
{name} spends a stroke on the drum. The drum does not notice.
The crank goes over. {name} waits with the rest.
broken: The pan stops coming round. It hangs open.
A delver wedges the crank. The mouth stays where it is.
The turning drags and catches. The opening holds.
The drum is stuck mid-turn. Now it can be hit.
fall: Onceround is down. The crank turns once more and stops.
The drum stands open at last.
The sugared lumps lie in the bowl, going cold.
No more waiting. Hands down.
Nothing swings by now. It is only iron.
The pan did not choose to be shut. It was built so.
Count the arms and go on.
Leave the bowl. There is nothing in it for you.

arrive: Something ahead is walking on poles, and one is gone.
A man, twice a man's height, crossing the room on a single stilt.
The other leg ends in a bound cuff and a splintered stump, hanging clear of the floor.
A crutch under the arm, where the leg should be. He leans on it the way you would.
He is quick. He has had time to learn the one pole.
Fen wool, wet through. Poles blackened with the water they were made to cross.
The stilt that is left is plain to see. Break it and he comes down. Leave it and he stands over you.
Over the front line, down into whoever is behind it. He does not choose. The party does.
The cuffs are mended and the lashings are tight. Someone looked after these poles for years.
act: {name} strikes down past the line, at whoever stands behind it.
{name} plants the crutch and swings the long pole round.
The stilt takes a step and the whole room moves with it.
{name} leans on the crutch and looks over your heads.
{name} reaches over the front line and finds the back.
The stump swings free. {name} does not look at it.
One pole, one crutch. {name} is steady on both.
broken: The stilt snaps. He comes down hard, level with you now.
No more reach over the line. He is quicker than he was.
The pole is gone and the man is at your height. He has nothing left to break.
Shorter stride, faster feet. Breaking it worked, and it cost you.
fall: Downfast is down. The crutch skids away across the floor.
The last pole lies where it fell.
He was already down one. Now he is down.
A man on poles, in a marsh, for his living. The poles are all that is left.
Count the party. Count the ones behind the line.
Leave the cuffs. They were bound by someone who cared.
The stump hung clear of the floor to the end.
Nobody asked him to walk on one leg. Go on.

arrive: A lamp on a belt, shuttered, and a man bent under a tub.
He has a long scoop in one hand and the pan of it resting on the floor.
The tub is full and he does not set it down.
There is one light on him. Everything else is wool and tar.
The shutter is on the lamp where a hand could reach it.
He works in the dark. When the light comes he stops.
Open the shutter and he stands still. Shut it and he is working again.
Nobody is hurt while the lamp is lit. Nobody is safe while it is dark.
Clean boots to the thigh and a tub that is rinsed. Someone gave this man the cellar and he kept it well.
act: The shutter is down. {name} is already somewhere else.
{name} drags the scoop. It was not where you swung.
In the dark, {name} works and the party pays.
The pan scrapes the floor. {name} does not look up.
{name} fills the tub, and moves on, and the room is a little emptier.
No light, no hurry. {name} has done this a thousand nights.
{name} steps out of the dark and back into it.
broken: The shutter is open. {name} stands with the tub on his hip and does nothing.
Lamp lit. He waits. Nothing you do to him will land.
A man in a lit room, standing still. It is not a trick.
Light on him and he stops. The same light means you cannot touch him.
fall: Nightwork is down. The tub tips and the lamp rolls clear.
The scoop lies where it fell, pan to the floor.
He worked in the dark so the cells would stay clean.
The lamp is still lit. Leave it that way a while.
A man with a tub, a scoop and a lamp. That was all he carried.
Nobody thanked him. The floor was swept.
Nightwork is down. The shutter is open and nobody has to close it.
The cellar is clear. Go on up.

arrive: The walls are sweating. It is getting colder, and the cold has a shape.
A squat man, bent double under a rack of cut blocks, tongs in the near hand.
Four pale blocks stacked up a dark frame, and a fifth hanging in the tongs.
Count them. You can do it from the door.
He is not coming for anyone. He is carrying.
While a block stands, the room is cold and everything in it is slow. Him as well.
The blocks go one at a time, in their own time. Nothing done to them hurries one.
Every round of cold is a round you were given. Spend it.
Wet wool, a good frame, boots mended at the toe. The ice was cut this morning and it shows.
act: A block lets go of the stack. {name} feels the room get no warmer.
{name} swings and the arm comes through slow. So does everyone's.
The rack creaks. {name} counts what is left on it.
{name} breathes out and can see it.
{name} reaches the tongs and the cold is already there.
Four blocks. Then three. {name} had better be somewhere by then.
The fifth swings in the tongs. {name} watches it and not the man.
broken: The last block goes. The room starts to thaw.
He sets the tongs down. He is not carrying any more.
The cold is off the room. He turns round.
Nothing took the stack down. It ran out, and now he is yours.
fall: Hoarback is down. The rack comes off his back and the frame lies still.
The tongs are on the floor. There is nothing in them.
He carried it down here so the cellars would keep.
Water on the flags, going warm. That is all that is left of the stack.
A man with a rack, a pair of tongs and a day's cutting. That was what he had.
Nobody thanked him. The meat kept.
Hoarback is down. You can feel your hands again.
The cold lifts. Go on up.

arrive: A wheel stood on the floor, taller than the man beside it. A rim, half-shod.
Tall, grey, one hand up on the rim. A hammer hanging in the other.
Four strakes of new iron lie ready on the tread. The nails are bright.
Count the strakes. That is the work he is still waiting on.
He is not looking at you. He is looking at the next strake.
The wheel is not finished. He will not call it finished for one pair of hands.
Old wool, old boots, a cap gone dark with sweat. The iron is the only new thing here.
Somebody started a rim here and nobody has put a blow into it but him.
He waits with the hammer held down over the strake. He has all day.
act: The hammer comes down on the rim. {name} hears the strake ring.
{name} strikes him and he does not move off the wheel.
{name} swings. The hand on the rim stays where it is.
He keeps the count. {name} is on it now, whatever else.
The hammer lifts and waits over the next strake. {name} knows what it is waiting for.
{name} lands one and he nods, once, as at a nail well set.
Four strakes on the tread. {name} counts what is left to strike.
broken: Every hand has struck the rim. The last blow goes in.
The last strake is home. He lets go of the wheel.
The hammer comes down for the last time and it is not his arm that moves it.
Nothing was done to him. The rim was finished, by all of you, and now he is yours.
fall: The Everyhand is down. The hammer rests on the floor and the wheel stands.
The wheel is whole. It will go where it is wanted.
He had a rim to shoe and he would not shoe it alone.
Four bright strakes, set and sound. Good iron, well laid.
A tall man, a hammer and a wheel to finish. That was all he had.
Nobody asked who struck the first blow. Everybody had.
The Everyhand is down. Your arm remembers the hammer.
The nails are in. Go on up.

arrive: A man stood in the middle of the floor with a bar across his shoulders. A pan hung off each end.
The bar is not level. One pan rides up by his shoulder and one hangs down by his knee.
Both pans are scoured bright. They are the cleanest things in the room.
Old coat, black with handling. Boots set wide. He is holding a load up and he is not walking.
He is not looking at you. He is looking at which pan is lower.
Put your weight in one pan and the other comes up. He will pay it back from there.
Stand where you like. The bar goes where the room goes.
The town's own standard, sealed and hung. Somebody trusted it once, and it is still true.
He waits, and the beam waits with him. Neither one is in a hurry.
act: The low pan sinks a hand's breadth. {name} feels the blow come back from the other side.
{name} strikes the heavy pan and the light one pays it out again.
The bar tips. {name} is standing under the wrong end of it.
{name} swings and the beam does not care how hard.
Both pans swing and settle. {name} looks at which one is up.
One side rises and the armour rises with it. {name} had put everything on the other.
{name} steps across the floor and the pans move with the step.
The chains creak. {name} watches the bar and not the man.
broken: The pans come level. The bar stops creaking.
Both sides are even. The last blow goes in and counts.
He stands straight under it for the first time. The beam is true.
Nothing was struck down. It was brought level, and now he is yours.
fall: Trueweight is down. The beam lies across the floor and the pans sit flat.
Both pans are on the flags, level. Nothing is hanging from either.
He carried the standard down here so the weights would stay honest.
Two bright pans, one beam, one man to hold it up. That was all he had.
Nobody was in a hurry to say which side had won.
Even on both sides. That is the only way it ever came down.
Trueweight is down. Your shoulders ache as if you had carried it.
The beam is true. Go on up.

arrive: A man stood in the middle of the floor with a sieve held low in both hands. It was the size of a cartwheel.
The sieve is pale as new bread. Black bars cross it both ways.
Flour on his coat to the elbow. Flour on the flags where he has been standing.
He is not looking at you. He is looking at what comes through.
A fine pale dust lies in front of him. Nothing else in the room is dusty.
He holds it level and does not hurry. Whatever comes to the bars is caught there.
A hood, a floured coat, long legs gone stooped from years of leaning over the work.
The bars are black and close. A small hand would fit between them. A big one would not.
He waits with the sieve down at his belt. He has sifted worse than you.
act: {name} swings hard and the blow stops dead on the bars. Flour jumps off the sieve.
The sieve takes it. {name} feels nothing come back, and nothing go through.
{name} strikes light and the blow goes between the bars.
A fine dust lifts. {name} cannot tell what was caught and what got by.
{name} puts everything into it. The bars do not so much as ring.
He shakes the sieve once, level. {name}'s strength lies spent on the pale face of it.
{name} steps in close. He does not turn. The sieve was already there.
The mesh is fine and he is patient. {name} is standing in the dust.
broken: A light blow went through the bars, and then another. He stops shaking the sieve.
The last blow goes through clean. The mesh did not catch it.
He looks down at what came through. It is a small thing, and it is enough.
Nothing was broken. It passed, and now he is yours.
fall: Finepass is down. The sieve lies on the flags, pale side up.
The bars are black and the dust is settling. Nothing is left in the mesh.
He sifted the floor so that what stayed would be worth keeping.
A hood, a sieve and a floured coat. That was all he had.
Nobody could say which blow had done it. They had all gone in quietly.
Fine as flour, and not a grain of it wasted.
Finepass is down. Your hands are floured to the wrist.
The mesh is clear. Go on up.

arrive: A man stood leaning into two traces in the middle of the floor. Behind him, something dragged.
The harrow is a dark lattice, low and raked. Bright tines stand down out of it into the flags.
The traces run from the front corners of the frame up over his shoulders into his fists.
Old field iron, black with years. The tines are the only clean thing on it. The ground did that.
He is pitched forward over his feet, the way a man walks into a hill.
The flags behind him are scored in long pale lines. Some of them are fresh.
He is not looking at you. He is looking at the end of the room, and the way to it.
A plain coat, the colour of old oats. A hat pulled low. He has walked this round before.
Something is being dragged across the floor, and he does not mean to stop for it.
act: {name} strikes and the blow lands. He does not turn. The traces do not slacken.
{name} stands to meet the harrow. The tines go by and {name} goes with them.
The round comes on. {name} had thought the harrow was behind him.
{name} swings hard. The pass is already half done and the swing changes none of it.
{name} steps aside and the lattice goes through the place where {name} stood.
The frame creaks and the tines bite the flags. {name} is on the wrong side of it.
{name} cuts at the traces and the traces hold. He leans and the harrow follows.
{name} is let go at the far end of the pass, a long way from where {name} began.
broken: A hard blow catches him in the traces and he does not break stride.
He pauses at the end of a pass, hands full, and then he takes up the round again.
The tines are dull for a moment, and then the floor makes them bright.
Nothing was stopped. It went by, and the room is different for it.
fall: Overturn is down. The harrow lies where it was dropped, tines in the air.
The traces are slack. The flags are scored from wall to wall, and they are still.
He worked the floor so that what lay under it could come up.
A hat, a pair of traces and a harrow. That was all he had.
He never once turned his head. He had a round to finish.
Turned over and left. That is how a field is made ready.
Overturn is down. Your boots are in the wrong place and you do not remember walking there.
The round is done. Go on up.

arrive: A stooped man stood in the middle of the floor under a board slung high off his shoulders. Someone was tied to it.
The board is raked back off him. A hooded figure lies along it, head at the top, feet bound at the bottom.
Three lashings cross the pledge. The rope is new, pale as straw. Everything else on him is old.
A strap runs from each lower corner of the board, over a shoulder and into a fist. He cannot put it down.
Old harness, old board, scuffed to the grain. The rope was cut today.
He is not looking at you. He is listening for whether you will swing.
The pledge moves. It is alive, and it is not walking.
A pledge taken against the town's debt. He has carried it a long way to be here.
Whatever this room pays out is on that board. It is whole. Nobody has hurt it yet.
act: {name} strikes the man. The board jolts, and so does what is tied to it.
{name} swings and the blow goes into both of them. The two are one load.
{name} hits hard. The pledge was tied to the man, and the blow counts for both.
{name} stops with the blow half thrown. The board hangs there, still.
{name} cuts a lashing. No blood. The rope parts and hangs loose.
The man staggers under it and does not put it down. {name} stands back.
{name} goes round behind and the board goes round too. Every side is the same side.
{name} looks at the ropes, then at the man. Whichever is hit, the load feels it.
broken: He staggers under the load and stays up.
He stoops lower. The board creaks and holds.
The straps bite into his shoulders. He does not let go of them.
Whatever he takes, the board takes some of it.
fall: Heldfast is down. The board lies on the flags beside him.
The straps are slack. The load is on the floor, and somebody has to look at it.
He carried it down here and never once set it down.
A harness, a board and three lengths of rope. That was all he had.
He never said what he was carrying it for.
Whoever stood closest will know what was on the board.
Heldfast is down. You are standing very still, the way he was.
The board is down. Go on up.

arrive: A man stood in the middle of the floor with a muster board slung off one shoulder and a hook in the other hand.
The board is dark wood with nine sockets cut in rows. Most are empty. One peg in it is pale.
Four old pegs sit grey in the board. They were taken before you came.
The pale peg has a tag hung off it. The tag is blank. It is waiting for a name.
A plain coat to the knee and a strap across the chest. His brow sits low and does not move.
The hook is bright where the rest of him is dull. It has been used often.
He keeps the board turned out to the side, in the open. He wants it seen.
Leather loops hang along the frame, one by every socket. A berth for each man signed.
He does not speak. He is looking along your line and counting, the way a sergeant counts.
act: {name} is taken by the collar. The hook goes in and does not tear.
{name} is signed. The pale peg takes a name and the tag turns over.
{name} turns round and swings at the party. The blade is the same blade. It is on the other side.
{name} goes for the man. The hook comes up and puts the signed one between them.
{name} stops with the blow half thrown. It is one of your own on the other end of it.
{name} reaches the board. The pale peg is a hand's width off and the tag swings.
{name} strikes the peg. The tag goes slack and the name is blank again.
{name} is on the roll now. Nobody asked {name}.
broken: The board takes a blow and rings. The pegs stay in.
He steps back with the board turned out. He does not hide it.
The hook comes up empty and goes down again.
A peg shifts in its socket. It is not the pale one.
fall: Oneshort is down. The board leans on the wall, pegs and all.
The hook is on the flags. It is bright still.
He signed names. That was the whole of his trade.
A board, a hook and a coat. That was all he had.
He never said whose names were on the old pegs.
The tag hangs from the pale peg, blank.
Oneshort is down. You count the party twice and the count is right.
The roll is closed. Go on up.

arrive: A man stood under a cracked roof with a timber on his shoulder. The timber went up into the dark and did not come down.
The prop is a round trunk, black with damp. It bows in the middle. It has been bowing a long time.
Three spare props lean at his back, each on a different rake. Raw ends. Nobody has set them.
Two pale wedges are driven in at the foot of the prop. They are the only bright thing in the room.
Boards lie crosswise along the top of it, three, grey and split. The roof rests on the boards.
One shoulder is under the timber. One hand is on it. The other arm hangs.
Dust comes down off the gallery in a thin line. It has not stopped since you came in.
He does not turn. He is listening to the roof, the way a miner listens.
Something in here is holding the roof up.
act: {name} strikes the man. The timber shudders and dust comes off the beams.
{name} stops with the blow half thrown. The roof ticks overhead.
{name} takes a spare prop and drives it home. The bow in the big timber eases a hair.
{name} gets a boot on a wedge. It shifts. The man's shoulder sags under it.
{name} knocks a wedge out. It rings off the stone. The prop goes slack by a finger.
{name} looks up, then down. Every blow here is aimed at the roof.
{name} sets the second prop. Two of three. The man breathes out.
{name} holds back. The man holds on. Neither moves, and the dust keeps falling.
broken: The timber groans and takes the weight again.
A board along the top splits. The roof does not come down.
He shifts his feet. The prop is no lower.
A wedge creeps in its seat. The rest hold.
fall: Deadfall is down. Nobody moves for a breath.
Look up before you look at him.
The spares stand where they were put, or they lie where they fell.
A timber, a shoulder pad and three boards. That was the whole of him.
He never said how long he had been holding it.
Dust still comes off the beams. It is slowing.
Deadfall is down. The roof ticks once more, then is quiet.
Go on out. Do not lean on anything.

arrive: A short man in a wide hat stood by a heap of earth as tall as himself. The heap was warm. Heat came off it in a slow shimmer.
The heap is turf and damp dirt, laid over cordwood and pressed flat with a spade. It has been earthed this week.
Eight stakes are driven round it, a withy lashed about their heads. They hold the earth where it wants to slump.
Small mouths are cut in the earth on the near side. Each has a dull red eye in it. They are breathing.
A rack of pale plugs stands beside the vents, new-split wood, clean as bread. One for every mouth.
A long tail of spoil runs out across the floor from the foot of the heap. He has been digging for a while.
Iron on the stakes and a leather apron down his front. The shovel is the newest thing about him.
He does not look up. He is watching the vents, not you. He is watching how they glow.
Something in here is shut on a fire.
act: {name} swings full weight at the heap. The earth takes it. A vent flares and the heat leans on the room.
{name} holds the stroke short. The earth shivers and stays shut.
{name} takes a plug off the rack and drives it into a mouth. The red eye goes out.
{name} puts a boot to a stake. The withy creaks and the earth holds.
{name} winds up for a big one. The man's shovel comes round and rests on the heap. He is waiting to see.
{name} strikes the man. It is a small blow and a clean one. The heap does not notice.
{name} seats another plug. One more red eye goes out. The man grips his haft.
{name} stops. The vents breathe. Nobody swings.
broken: A vent coughs. Smoke comes up in a thin line and thins out.
He sets the shovel against the earth and leans. The heap settles.
A stake leans. He knocks it straight with the flat of the blade.
The heat does not rise. He lets out his breath.
fall: Halfblow is down. The heap ticks and settles.
Look at the vents before you look at him.
The plugs stand in the rack, or they are in the earth. They are not in the fire.
A hat, an apron and a shovel. That was the whole of him.
He never said how long it had been burning.
Smoke comes off the heap in a thin line. It is slowing.
Halfblow is down. The red eyes dim one by one.
Go on out. Walk soft. Nothing here needs hurrying.

arrive: A tall man in a clean grey coat stood at the far end of the bench. He had his back to the work.
The coat is good cloth, buttoned to the throat. He is a man who gets paid to watch other people.
His head is turned hard off his shoulders. It is not turned at you. It is turned along the room.
One pale mitt is held out level, as if along a rule. It points at somebody.
Follow the mitt. It stops on one of you. Look at who.
He is not looking at the one in front. He is not looking at the one who has hit him most.
He does not hurry. He has the cold patience of a man checking a tally.
Move, and the mitt moves with you. Then it settles again.
Somebody in here is being counted.
act: {name} hits him and the mitt does not come round. It stays where it was.
{name} steps back to heal and the mitt comes round to {name}.
{name} holds the shot. The cold eyes find {name} and stay.
{name} breaks off for a flask. The mitt is level on {name} before the cork is out.
{name} has carried the fight. He does not look at {name}.
{name} swings once, hard. The mitt lifts off and goes looking.
The mitt swings to the back of the room and stops. {name} is standing in it.
{name} stands still. The head does not turn. Somebody else is being watched.
broken: The mitt wavers. He does not know who it is.
He turns his whole shoulders to look. The mitt sags.
A long wait. The mitt comes up slow.
He lowers it and starts again from the near end.
fall: Velrick is down. The mitt drops to his side.
He did not raise his voice. He did not need to.
The head comes round at last. It is facing the floor.
Nobody is being watched now.
A grey coat on the boards. Good cloth, still clean.
Look who is standing where you are.
Whoever you were behind is not behind you any more.
Go on out. Nobody is counting.

arrive: A man in a scorched coat stood with a basket of fire held at his chest in both hands.
The coat has stood at a hearth for years. The hearth has come with him.
Four pale vanes stand out of the basket rim. They are the only pale thing on him.
He is not tall. Standing alone, he does not look like much.
The fire in the basket sits low and red. It is waiting to see how many of you there are.
He does not pick a target. He does not need to.
Come in one at a time and it stays low. Come in together and you will feel it.
The draught is not his. The draught is whoever is standing in reach.
Four vanes. Count them from the door.
act: {name} steps in beside the others. The red goes orange.
{name} is the only one in reach. The fire stays low and red. It will take all day.
One more delver in reach and the basket brightens. That is the draught.
{name} swings. The hearth answers the whole line, not only {name}.
{name} stands off and does not come in. The fire drops a shade.
The line closes on him. White heat. It answers every one of them.
{name} breaks a vane off the rim. It stays broken.
Everybody in, the habit says. {name} is in. The fire is up.
broken: A vane is gone from the rim. It will not be put back.
Fewer vanes, and the fire has less to draw on.
He turns the basket to hide the gap. The gap is still there.
The rim is bare in places. The fire sits lower.
fall: He is down. The basket tips and the fire goes out on the boards.
No draught now. The red goes to grey.
He kept the hearth high to the end. It was his to carry.
A scorched coat and an empty basket.
It burned as hard as you crowded it. Nobody argues that.
The coat is still warm. It will not be for long.
Whoever stood closest felt it last.
Go on out. The room is cold.

arrive: A man in a flour-white smock stood under a hopper bigger than he was, turned a little off the door.
The hopper is hooped like a barrel. A pale chute runs over his shoulder and down to a trough at his hip.
He is pouring. Fine meal comes down the chute and settles in the trough.
His face is a pale mask with a dark slot to breathe through. He has not looked up.
Nothing on him is alight. That is the point of him.
The air at the door is thick and tastes of flour. It does not get thicker. It does not need to.
Leave the fire hand at the door. Leave the lamp too, if you can spare it.
Whatever burns in here burns for everyone. Him included.
Mind the flour.
act: {name} throws fire. It lands on the whole line, and on him, all the same.
{name} keeps the fire hand in the pocket. Steel does the work. It is slow.
{name} sets the air off on purpose. Everybody burns. He burns with the rest.
{name} swings steel. The meal settles. Nothing catches.
{name} takes the burn and keeps swinging. It is quicker this way. Nobody says so.
A spark off {name}'s blade. The room answers, all of it.
{name} sets the lamp down by the wall. The air is easier.
{name} reaches for the flint, and thinks better of it.
broken: A hoop is gone from the hopper. Meal runs out of the gap and does not stop.
The chute runs thin. The trough sits lower than it did.
He braces the hopper with a shoulder. It leans anyway.
Less meal in the air. The same rule holds.
fall: He is down. The hopper tips and the meal goes across the boards.
The chute runs dry. The trough is empty.
He poured to the end. It was his work.
A white smock and a split hopper.
The air stays thick a while. Wait before you light anything.
Whoever burned the most knew it. So did he.
He never lifted a hand. The room did the rest.
Open the door. Let it clear.

arrive: Something ahead has been over this room with reed.
A man in a dark hood stood at the back with a bound sheaf of cut stems across his shoulder.
Every body in the room is thatched. Roof-deep, close and tidy, the way a good hand lays it.
He has a flat board at his hip and a handle in his fist. He is not looking at you. He is looking at the work.
The hood has no face worth the name. The sheaf is neat, tied in three places.
Strike the ones in front and the blow lands in straw. It lands in straw every time.
He is not hitting anyone. He does not need to.
The roof stays on while he stands. Walk past the others and reach him.
Mind the reed. Count the ties.
act: {name} strikes the nearest. The blow goes into straw and stops.
{name} cuts through the thatch. A handful comes away. The rest holds.
{name} goes round the others. The hooded man is at the back.
{name} beats at the roof. It sheds the weather and the steel alike.
The line pushes forward. The thatch takes it all, and gives nothing back.
{name} aims for the man at the back and not the room. It is the only blow that counts.
Straw flies. The one under it is not marked.
{name} spends a good while on straw. Nobody says it was wasted. It was.
broken: A tie is cut on the sheaf. The stems splay and do not close.
A bare patch shows on the roof, and it does not grow back.
He sets the leggett to the thatch and beats it flat. It is thinner than before.
Fewer stems on his shoulder. He works as if there were plenty.
fall: He is down. The sheaf comes apart on the boards.
The thatch goes off the room all at once, like a roof lifted off.
Every body in there is bare now. They can be hurt, and they know it.
A dark hood and a loose bundle of cut stems.
He laid the whole roof himself. It came off with him.
Nothing was ever protecting itself. It was all him.
Dry reed and a leggett on the floor.
Sweep the straw back. Then go in.

_note_c100: C-100: STAND-DOWN, gap zero at 25 minibosses, no 26th landed. Audit of the 29 trick-only lord shape lines refused at D97 (bosses.json lesser_uniques/greater_uniques; names, shapes and skews are spoken, the trick is not built). ALL 29 STATE A MECHANIC AS FACT. Not reworded here (additive only; edit needs Mr. E). READS AS A PROMISE, A: tells the viewer what to DO, so acting and seeing nothing is a lie - Vestry-Kept (strike the lantern), Kettle-Drummed (break the drummer), Ditch-Silted (hit it as it turns), Lamp-Shy (light drives her off), Hearth-Fooled (draw it off), Lamp-Oiled (one spark). B: states a hard rule of the fight that is checkably false - Gable-Cling (nothing reaches it), Charter-Sworn (strikes what crosses its ring), Well-Chained (cannot cross the room), Barn-Wide (cannot be gone round), Chaperoned (each takes one blow). C: the other 18 state a trigger or effect that does not fire; weaker, same defect. PROPOSED FLAVOUR-ONLY REPLACEMENTS for A and B, each claims no mechanic and keeps the skew: Vestry-Kept: 'it keeps one small flame close, like a keepsake - smaller for it, and meaner'. Kettle-Drummed: 'a drum beats behind them - the host comes on to the count'. Ditch-Silted: 'caked in ditch-mud - heavy, slow, and in no mood'. Lamp-Shy: 'she keeps to the dark and does not care for the lamps'. Hearth-Fooled: 'it came up toward a light and has been angry since'. Lamp-Oiled: 'oil on every bone, and the smell of it down the whole floor'. Gable-Cling: 'it keeps to the wall and comes down late'. Charter-Sworn: 'it keeps one spot and holds it'. Well-Chained: 'chained at the neck to a well-head, dragging the weight'. Barn-Wide: 'wide as a barn door, and as hard to shift'. Chaperoned: 'two grey attendants walk behind her and say nothing'. CODE/OWNER WIRING: none new. Decision for Mr. E or the supervisor: swap these 11 shape strings in bosses.json (one shape string each, hp/speed/attack untouched), or build the tricks. Until then A and B are the lines most likely to be caught on stream.

stairs_up: One flight up. The next is the same flight.
The stair is long and it only goes one way.
Up, a step at a time. Nothing carries them.
spent: They are spent. The stair does not care.
Nothing left in the legs. The stair is still there.
They sit on a step and breathe, then go on.
out: Daylight. The gate is a gate again.
Out. The air smells of the river.
The door at the top is only a door. They go through it.
wipe: Nobody came up. The gate stayed open a while.
The stair is empty. Somebody lit a lamp for it anyway.

encumbered: {name} shifts the pack and goes on, slower.
The straps bite. {name} does not stop.
heavily_encumbered: {name} breathes like a bellows. The pack does not care.
{name} is one bad step from the floor.
{name} has stopped looking at the walls. Only the next stair.
pickup: {name} takes {item}. The pack gets a little worse.
{item} into the pack. {name} pretends it weighs nothing.
over_capacity: They cannot take all of it, and everyone knows which pile is theirs.
The stair is going to decide this for them.
left_behind: {item} stays on floor {floor}. {name} will not say it was easy.
{name} leaves {item} on floor {floor}. The back wins.
dropped_stays: {item} is on floor {floor} yet. The dark has not taken it.
come_back: {name} goes down again for {item}. The stair does not get shorter.
They climb back for {item}. It had better be worth it.
greed: The floor will still be there tomorrow. Your back may not.
Every extra pound is a day you do not get.
Ask what it weighs before you ask what it is worth.

deposit: {item} goes in the vault. {name} signs the page.
{name} lets {item} go to the {hall}. The clerk takes it in both hands.
withdraw: {name} collects {item} from the {hall}. It is as they left it.
The clerk brings {item} up from the vault. {name} signs again.
full: The clerk at the {hall} shakes their head. There is no shelf.
Full. The {hall} would take it if it could.
raised: Shelves at the {hall}, new wood. {who} paid.
The vault has grown. {who} has a line in the ledger.
death_kept: {name} will not come for it. The vault keeps it for the next.
The vault does not ask who is alive. It keeps what it was given.
inventory: Pack {n} of {m}, {w} carried. Vault: {v}, at the {hall}.
{v} in the vault. {w} on the back. {n} of {m} places in the pack.

placed: {name} takes {item} to the {shop}. Somebody has to buy it.
{item} goes under {name}'s arm and down the street to the {shop}.
sold: {n} gold at the {shop}. {item} is somebody else's now.
{name} sells {item} for {n} and puts the coin away without counting.
The {shop} pays {n}. {name} takes it and goes.
refused_level: The {shop} is too small to buy {item}. It says so politely.
{item} is too good for this counter. {name} walks it home.
No shop this size has the coin. {name} knows it already.
worn_below: {name} is still wearing it. The shop can wait.
It cannot be sold while it is on a hero's back, and the hero is below.

bought: {name} bought a stone. It is smaller than it sounds.
A stone in the pocket and {name} walks a little easier.
shatters: The stone breaks. {name} is not on the floor any more.
{name} crushes the stone. The floor lets go. {name} is in the square, breathing hard.
one_hero: The stone took {name}. The others did not get a vote.
One stone. One hero. The rest hold the line.
lords_floor: The stone breaks and the floor holds. A lord is on it.
{name} breaks the stone on a lord's floor. It is the wrong floor.
panic: Break it now. That is the whole instruction.
The stone is for this second and no other.

interrupted: {name} was on the way for {item}. The way is not clear.
The errand stops. Something is in the road.
{name} sets the order down and draws instead.
level_changed: The town grew while {name} walked. The order has changed with it.
{name} reaches the {shop}. It is a bigger shop than it was.
waits_below: The order waits while {name} is below. {item} will keep.
{name} cannot walk it while they are down. It waits.
